title: Council Post: Three Data Management And Protection Predictions For 2024
text:
Simon Jelley, General Manager for SaaS Protection, Endpoint and Backup Exec at Veritas Technologies.
With 2024 upon us, what better time to look into the metaphorical crystal ball and discuss some of the key trends that will impact businesses in the new year? Given my expertise in data management and protection, that’s where I’ll focus. Here are three predictions I believe leaders should be aware of.
1. LLMs will transform your data practices.
If you’re like most business leaders, you probably had never heard the term large language model (LLM) before 2023. But thanks in large part to the meteoric rise of highly accessible generative artificial intelligence (AI) like OpenAI’s ChatGPT in late 2022 and 2023, it’s now seared into our lexicons. Still, it may behoove us to briefly explore what an LLM is.
Language modeling is a form of machine learning used in AI in which a computer system analyzes existing bodies of text and then determines the probability of a sequence of words occurring in a sentence. Large language models (LLMs) are language modeling to the extreme. As the word “large” indicates, LLMs are a form of AI based on massive data sets, so big that they can self-generate entirely new, original content that’s virtually indistinguishable from something a human created.
The increasing demand to use LLMs to improve business efficiency will likely impact data practices in several ways in 2024.
• Better Capture, Classification And Cleaning Of Data: In my last article, I talked about how while "sound human decision-making depends on complete and accurate understanding, machine learning relies on complete, organized and accurate—what you might call ‘good’—data. Without it, even the best algorithms are useless.” Given the vast amount of data modern organizations produce, this means you may have to invest in additional IT staff and tools to improve the amount of “good” data you have to build reliable LLMs on.
• Evolved Data Compliance: Most regulatory agencies are currently investigating how to best apply existing data privacy laws to LLMs. However, as legitimate generative AI business use cases increase, it is likely that new data privacy legislation will be introduced that applies guardrails specifically to LLMs and their training data sets.
• Stronger Data Governance: Finally, you’ll need stronger data governance to better control data silo sprawl and secure data in motion. In my experience, this is best done with automated data classification and life cycle management. You may also need to consider hiring a Chief Data Officer to better bridge the gap between your IT and legal teams.
2. AI will make the cyber threat landscape even more dangerous.
LLMs and other forms of AI aren’t exclusive to the good guys. As I previously stated, “AI chatbots like ChatGPT and the technology behind them could usher in a golden age of cybercrime where even the least technical criminals turn to pilfering data for profit.” In fact, cybercriminals are already taking advantage of AI. They're using platforms like WormGPT to up their social engineering game and make things like phishing emails more persuasive than anything we’ve seen before. It’s not out of the realm of possibility that in 2024, we’ll see the first fully AI-driven ransomware threats that can attack with startling efficacy, efficiency and little to no human involvement.
To combat this threat, consider increasing your investment in cyber preparedness with cross-functional teams who can identify, assess, recommend and test organizational-, social- and IT-driven potential weaknesses.
But even that may not be enough. Recent Veritas Technologies research found that "more than two-thirds of organizations are looking to boost their cyber resiliency with the help of AI." Already, AI-powered malware detection, self-healing data sets and data identification and classification are being employed as data resiliency solutions. In 2024, further advancements in AI-driven autonomous data management should help organizations fight fire with fire and continue defending against ever-evolving ransomware threats.
3. Cost pressures will continue to affect cloud transformation.
As a business leader, you’re undoubtedly acutely aware of the economic uncertainty we’ve been living and working under. While, thankfully, the economy was resilient enough to avoid a recession in 2023, the jury is still out on whether we will eventually face one in 2024 or not.
That continued uncertainty leads me to reemphasize a prediction I made last year: Companies will likely look to cut costs by scaling back on current and new business transformation initiatives. Of that, I noted how current cloud transformations will likely continue, but some new cloud transformation initiatives may be put on hold until macroeconomic conditions improve.
The result is that in 2024, just as in 2023, IT departments need to be prepared to continue managing hybrid multi-cloud environments with data spread equally across public clouds and on-premises data centers. The following steps I suggested last year still apply: Establish unified data observability, enable workload portability, leverage software-defined storage, prioritize data compliance and eliminate data protection silos.
Predicting the future isn’t an exact science, but preparing for these trends may help ensure your organization’s data management and protection strategy is ready for 2024 and beyond.

title: Council Post: 20 Tech Experts On The Tools And Trends That Will Dominate 2024
text:
If you ask anyone with even a passing interest in technology which tool captured the most headlines in 2023, they’d certainly name artificial intelligence (perhaps, more specifically, generative AI). Looking ahead into 2024, many tech leaders and watchers say AI will still dominate conversations and company initiatives; however, the focus will be not only on its extended capabilities, but also on its limitations—and even its consequences.
Still, even the powerhouse that is AI isn’t the only intriguing and exciting tech development experts predict for 2024. Below, 20 members of Forbes Technology Council share their predictions for the top tools and trends they see emerging and expanding in 2024 (including what’s next for AI), as well as how these developments could impact how we live and work.
1. AI
AI will continue to be a trending topic. Organizations that realize too late that AI models must be built on real-world, relevant business operational data will fall significantly behind their competitors. In essence, data is king. It’s what fuels innovation. If an enterprise wants competitive differentiation, it must leverage its own unique data—not just what’s readily available online. - Jamie Lerner, Quantum Corporation
2. Generative AI
We’ll continue to hear a lot about generative AI in 2024, because it’s the most disruptive technology since the internet. While 2023 was the year of AI creation and experimentation, 2024 will be the year organizations practically apply AI in their processes and practices, elevating it beyond just a marketing buzzword to a valuable solution that drives productivity and innovation. - Todd Fisher, CallTrackingMetrics
Forbes Technology Council is an invitation-only community for world-class CIOs, CTOs and technology executives. Do I qualify?
3. ‘AI Plus’
In 2024, we’ll see a lot of what I call “AI plus”—AI plus cloud; AI plus security; AI plus data science. Existing foundational tech skills will be enhanced through effective applications of AI, and AI skill sets will become more niche as technologists in every domain gain expertise in applying AI tools to their technology problems. This will represent a shift from AI adoption toward AI maturity. - Aaron Skonnard, Pluralsight
4. Customer 360
Customer 360 will be a top trend. Leveraging data will be core, followed by layering AI on top of the data to fully understand and know your customer. Every team across the company will have “single source of truth” access to information about a customer, from a question asked on the website to a product purchase to a service ticket—and beyond. - Terry Mirza, Compugen Systems, Inc.
5. Automation
Automation will take center stage in 2024, as IT teams are expected to do more with less. We’ll see this in action within the IT help desk. If businesses reduce the number of incidents, the volume of tickets reaching service desks will go down, cutting costs and giving time back to users. We’ll also see vendors focus on personalized customer service—specifically, providing concierge-style services. - Ian van Reenen, 1E
6. Protecting The Data Used By Generative AI
As the use of generative AI expands, effective cybersecurity is even more essential. In many cases, generative AI algorithms depend on either proprietary data from the company developing the program or data generated directly from users. By moving processing to the edge, sensitive data can be analyzed at the source rather than at a data center, where there is greater risk of a security breach. - Christine Boles, Intel
7. Proprietary AI Agents
Now that companies have explored foundational AI applications, we’ll see the introduction of proprietary AI agents to manage all of the AI tools a company has deployed across the organization. These autonomous agents will interface between humans and tools—equipped with the ability to speak the language of both—streamlining workflows and creating entirely new ones between humans and their new AI colleagues. - Marco Santos, GFT
8. Deceptive Marketing About AI
AI is going to be marketed as being embedded in everything we use, but these claims will be partly snake oil. For example, AI may be used in the design, marketing or sale of a product, but not in the product itself. “AI” will be the new “turbo”—a common marketing term of the 1980s and ’90s that literally meant nothing. - Peter Gregory, GCI Communications
9. Decentralized Finance
In 2024, many people may be talking a lot about new ways to handle money utilizing computer systems—collectively dubbed “decentralized finance” or “DeFi”—and specifically, blockchain. These developments may make it easier for everyone to borrow, invest and undertake other financial transactions without relying on large banks. It’s changing the way we manage money. - Neelima Mangal, Spectrum North
10. Dark AI As A Service
In 2024, we’ll see the emergence of dark AI as a service. Global threat actors will call upon a ChatGPT-like solution to craft malicious attacks inclusive of the recommended target organization, custom malware, and bespoke phishing messages addressed to the correct organizational stakeholders. - Tim Femister, NetXperts
11. Immersive Learning Technologies
In the education realm, I anticipate the continued rise of immersive learning technologies, particularly virtual and augmented realities. These tools have the potential to transform traditional learning by creating engaging, interactive experiences that transport students to virtual worlds or enhance their real-world surroundings. Expect to see them integrated into various subjects, from history to science. - Shelli Brunswick, Space Foundation
12. Blending AI And Human Effort For Competitive Advantage
Artificial intelligence will fundamentally change nearly every aspect of business, from operations to revenue growth to customer experience to business model reinvention and more. Through its accessibility and scalability, AI can help companies get work done in more powerful ways. Those companies that are tech-powered and human-led can create a competitive advantage. - Matthew Lieberman, PwC
13. Dedicated AI Competency And Compliance Efforts
As machine learning continues to mature, large language models will consolidate as generative AI becomes a standard development tool—as ubiquitous as the cloud for enterprise operations. Organizations will need robust AI competency centers and dedicated compliance officers. The public will increasingly trust digital service touch points, and next-generation customer service levels will arise. - Nikola Mrksic, PolyAI
14. Brain-Computer Interfaces
In 2024, we can expect a surge in innovation associated with brain-computer interfaces due to ongoing developments in neurotechnology. Enhanced techniques for controlling devices directly through thoughts will lead to more immersive VR experiences and assist individuals with disabilities. However, such technologies may raise ethical and privacy concerns. - Cristian Randieri, Intellisystem Technologies
15. Instant Payment Systems
This year will see the dawn of the era of instant payments. The trend toward increased use of digital payments will accelerate as pay-by-bank and account-to-account transactions gain traction, reducing debit and credit card use and forcing an overhaul of traditional banking and merchant services business models. - Vivek Jetley, EXL
16. Faster Product Development Through GitHub Copilot
It’ll be interesting to see how the GitHub Copilot chat feature progresses throughout 2024. You can now write a full prompt, and Copilot takes into account more context about what you want to do, explains what needs to be done to accomplish that and why, and drafts a more complete code outline than ever before. The chat function improves efficiency, allowing tech teams to bring products to market faster. - Ryan Barone, RentRedi
17. Commonsense Tech Tools
Both industry insiders and regular people are tired of hearing about the “innovation economy.” They will be looking for tools and technology that promise to improve workflows, save money and time, and reduce friction. 2024 will be a year of commonsense tools for improving lives and operational outcomes, rather than lofty expectations and speculation. - Lewis Wynne-Jones, ThinkData Works
18. Reduced Funding For ‘AI Companies’
2023 was the year of AI. Yet, for every genuinely new idea, there have been five marketing tools or scheduling software suites that “run with AI.” In 2024, we will see many of these companies falter once VC funding for “AI companies” returns to matching the industry average. Consequently, in 2024 we will hear about “AI companies” failing—along with accompanying predictions about the end of AI. - Kevin Korte, Univention
19. Quantum Computing
IBM recently unveiled the first quantum computer, a potential landmark moment. Quantum computing will continue to be a major tech development as research becomes more solidified and actual applications develop. The impact that kind of computing power could have on various industries, from healthcare to finance, would be groundbreaking, and we’re on the cusp of finally breaking that ground. - Tal Frankfurt, Cloud for Good
20. Digital Twins
I believe 2024 will be the year of the digital twin—my team is tracking news coverage and analyst data weekly, and the number of articles increases every week. What is a digital twin? It’s a digital interface that allows operators to review, explore, decide and orchestrate the physical and digital aspects of their business at many levels. The great promise of the “single pane of glass” is finally here. - Jim Barrett, Edge Total Intelligence

title: How Samsung’s Galaxy S24 Ultra Will Change Smartphones Forever
text:
Updated January 8: article originally posted January 7
The upcoming Galaxy Unpacked event will set the standard for every flagship phone in 2024 to be measured against. The Galaxy S24 Ultra is Samsung’s bid to define the future of smartphones.
First, the Galaxy S24 Ultra must be the proverbial “really good phone.” There should be no obvious mistakes, nothing weaker than the opposition, and essentially everything a consumer expected from the leading Android flagship must be in the Galaxy S24 Ultra. Samsung’s iterative approach to the Ultra handsets means that the success of the S23 Ultra should easily carry on with the requisite upgrades in the specifications.
It’s also worth remembering that the S24 Ultra is part of a family of phones. There is a halo effect with the Galaxy S24 branding, which means the Galaxy S24 and Galaxy S24+ handsets also need to be up to standard—any issues with the handset lower down the portfolio will impact the S24 Ultra.
That’s one reason why the community is sensitive to the disparity between the Exynos and the Snapdragon chipsets used by the lower-tier models. Luckily for those wanting the ultimate power, the S24 Ultra will exclusively run the more respected Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 for Samsung.
Samsung’s popularity, interest from the press, and leadership role in the Android space will ensure the Galaxy S24 Ultra will be seen as the handset to beat for future flagships.
Update: Monday January 8. During the company's CES Press Conference, Samsung outlined its wider vision of AI in technology. Titled “AI For All - Connectivity In The Age Of AI,” Samsung Device Experience CEO Jong-He ‘JH’ Han introduced several partners and devices that will bring AI to consumers.
The traditional meme of the Internet Connected Fridge has been updated with the "Refrigerator With AI Family Hub,” offering a 32-inch display reporting on the products the AI recognizes inside the fridge with recipe suggestions and tracking of use-by dates. A similar AI hub is part of the Laundry Combo, offering AI in a washer and dryer.
On the consumer electronics side, Samsung took the opportunity to showcase the AI features in its recently launched Galaxy Book4 laptop. While there was no specific mention of the Galaxy S24 family, the entire presentation had a smartphone-shaped hole in it.
A hole that will be packed by the upcoming Galaxy Unpacked event.
The upcoming Galaxy Unpacked event will lean heavily toward using artificial intelligence on the smartphone. If you haven't seen the signs, the invitation screaming "Galaxy AI is coming” gives the game away. The South Korean company is not going into the event cold. Its Samsung Gauss AI system was given an official launch at the end of 2023
Several specific AI features have already been trailed around the camera, Zoom with Galaxy AI was showcased in the teaser videos ahead of the Galaxy Unpacked events. More importantly, both Qualcomm and Samsung have ensured that the respective Snapdragon and Exynos chipsets have dedicated hardware to enhance AI and ML software routines.
Samsung’s Exynos joins and reinforces Qualcomm’s snapdragon, MediaTek's Dimensity, and Google’s Tensor in offering hardware support for AI and ML routines. That means the Galaxy S24, S24+, and S24 Ultra handsets—which could easily have used a different vision of hardware to achieve AI—will consolidate the market. This is how AI can be delivered across the Android ecosystem.
In all this, do not discount how comfortable consumers are buying a Samsung device. While Google’s launch of the Pixel 8 and Pixel 8 Pro handsets was built around the promise of AI, the market share of Pixel devices and Galaxy devices are not in the same ballpark. Samsung can bring AI to the broadest possible market around the world.
Consumers who walk into a store to “buy a new Samsung” will have AI in their hands, first with the S24 family and then throughout the year into the new Galaxy A handsets and the Galaxy Tabs. The practical impact of AI on photography will be part of OneUI, and the “Galaxy AI” will no doubt be mentioned throughout the launch and at every point-of-sale unit.
There’s another area where Samsung can set the standard going forward. The company could match Google’s promise of seven years of software and security updates across the Galaxy S range. Google has shown how attractive this is; now, Samsung can force itself to the front of the line in the broader consumer market.
Samsung’s focus on delivering AI, consumer confidence in the brand, and an extended support window for software and hardware is how the Galaxy S24 can shape the smartphone world in 2024.

title: New focus in military spending can keep Pentagon step ahead of China: expert
text:
New focus in military spending can keep Pentagon step ahead of China: expert
Some experts fear the possibility of 'runaway AI' on the battlefield
The 2024 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) includes a heavy focus on the continued development of artificial intelligence for the military, an investment that could be pivotal in the continued competition with China.
"I think there are two key areas of the NDAA that point to a great strategic direction for the United States. The first is recognizing the threat China poses in both the physical and the cognitive domain of conflict, in the cold war we are currently in with them and the hot war they may consider in the future. AI, and protecting AI is a crucial part of that strategic calculus," Christopher Alexander, the chief analytics officer of Pioneer Development Group, told Fox News Digital.
Alexander's comments come after President Biden signed the Pentagon spending bill into law last month, the yearly "must pass" legislation that lays out U.S. military spending.
WHAT IS ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE (AI)?
In the 2024 version of the spending plan, lawmakers made clear the importance of continued AI development for national defense. Perhaps most importantly, the bill created a new Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Officer Governing Council for the military, which will be in charge of oversight and the responsible development of AI technology for military use.
The new level of oversight was a promising development for some experts, who noted that many unknown dangers could be presented with the continued development of AI.
"It’s good to see Congress taking the AI revolution seriously by creating a new role at the Pentagon responsible for oversight," Jon Schweppe, policy director at American Principles Project, told Fox News Digital. "This is a first step, and obviously more will be needed in the coming months to ensure we are putting needed guardrails into place to prevent the 'runaway AI' problem."
Ziven Havens, the policy director of the Bull Moose Project, echoed similar sentiment, noting that this year's NDAA "contains 149 mentions of artificial intelligence" as the U.S. attempts to balance being a leader in the AI race with safety.
DEFENSE DEPARTMENT NEEDS WIDESPREAD AI ACQUISITION GUIDANCE, GOVERNMENT REPORT SAYS
"The most pressing is the creation of the Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Officer Governing Council," Havens told Fox News Digital. "While it is paramount that the U.S. maintains its global leadership of AI, doing so must be done responsibly."
In addition to the creation of new oversight mechanisms, the 2024 NDAA also lays out new AI initiatives for the Pentagon, including a requirement that the secretary of defense create a strategic plan for developing and using AI for defense.
But the increased focus on AI comes at a time of growing concern over the safety of the technology, something Biden has attempted to address with executive action in 2023.
"The government is in a precarious situation with artificial intelligence. On one hand, it cannot afford to slow down – particularly in the case of defense. On the other hand, as we saw with President Biden's recent executive order, it is making it increasingly difficult for people to develop tech that will allow the defense industry to flourish in the first place," Samuel Mangold-Lenett, a staff editor at The Federalist, told Fox News Digital. "There also remain questions about what the current administrative apparatus considers 'ethical use' and 'data-informed diplomacy,' in and of itself, is risky. We can't defer to machine learning on things that are ultimately issues of humanity. That said, it's good the government is taking AI's defense capabilities more seriously."
AI-POWERED COMBAT AIRCRAFT BRING US HUGE BATTLEFIELD ADVANTAGE BUT RAISE ETHICAL QUESTIONS
While this year's NDAA attempts to address such concerns with formal oversight, it makes clear that the U.S. will continue to charge ahead with recent military developments in AI, including a race toward autonomous weapons that could tilt the battlefield in future conflicts with rivals such as China.
One such weapon that has been in development since 2016 is the XQ-58A Valkyrie experimental aircraft, a stealth platform that can be operated by AI. The Pentagon hopes the plane, which saw its first test flight in 2019, will be able to provide an inexpensive weapon that can also limit human pilot losses or even serve to protect manned aircraft while in flight.
For Alexander, continued development of such systems will be key for the U.S. if it hopes to continue its military advantage over China.

"Autonomous vehicles essentially flip the script on our adversaries and give the U.S. an asymmetric advantage as inexpensive drones and other capabilities have near peer effectiveness against much more expensive, manned platforms."

"If we prepare the products we are currently producing well, pay attention to maximising investment efficiency and maintaining financial soundness, I think we can attempt to double the current market capitalisation of 100 trillion won to 200 trillion won within three years," Kwak said.
SK Hynix was ahead of rivals in developing the latest in high bandwidth memory (HBM) chips used in the fast-growing field of generative AI, securing AI-chip leader Nvidia as a client.
The chips, known as HBM3, can feed more data into chips used for generative AI, enabling them to compute at high speed.

Memory chip makers including SK Hynix and Samsung have engaged in extensive production cuts since early last year to weather the worst industry downturn in decades as high inflation dented demand for gadgets containing chips.

title: Council Post: Leadership In The Age Of AI: Being A Responsible Citizen
text:
Beena Ammanath - Global Deloitte AI Institute Leader, Founder of Humans For AI and Author of "Trustworthy AI" and "Zero Latency Leadership"
In this era of humans working with machines, being an effective leader with artificial intelligence (AI) takes a range of skills and activities. In this series, I provide an incisive roadmap for leadership in the age of AI.
For many businesses, AI is attractive because it affords efficiencies and capacity that drive the bottom line. Yet I believe the full potential of AI requires enterprise leaders to account for potentially negative outcomes, not just for the business but for everyone. The trustworthiness and ethics of AI depend in part on how it is used. As business leaders look for value-driving deployments and maximized business value, we also need to be mindful of the cascading impact an AI use case could have on society.
AI's Potential Impact On Society
This is a lesson learned repeatedly in the history of transformative technologies. To borrow from the cinematic gem Jurassic Park, we are sometimes so preoccupied with whether we could that we do not pause to consider whether we should. Within an organization, who asks the question, “What are the poor societal outcomes that could arise if we deploy this model?” While AI stakeholders are found throughout an organization, it is those in leadership who need to establish the importance of considering the broader impact AI can have on society.
Cautionary tales abound. For example, in the early days of the internet, organizations rushed in to capitalize on digital connectivity, sometimes with only a passing glance at the nascent idea of cybersecurity. We still grapple today with technology decisions that were made decades ago.
Now, organizations using AI to remove human bias from hiring decisions have discovered how bias in historical data can perpetuate the inequality the AI seeks to resolve. Facial recognition technology raises questions around fair treatment, privacy, safety and who should be permitted to use those systems and for which use case. AI-enabled chatbots that automate customer and citizen engagement have the potential to generate biased, inaccurate or even antagonistic outputs.
Social media platforms may monetize user data via targeted advertising, and one approach is fine-tuning recommendation algorithms for “attention retention.” Today, we know that a tangential result is the potential for social media platforms to create echo chambers and mental health risks.
Asking The Right Questions
Hindsight is 20/20, and some outcomes may not be obvious. Yet I believe the lesson is that when contending with powerful technologies at scale, business leaders should think as much about the near-term gains as they do the long-term impact of their programs. Now more than ever, let's scrutinize the models and use cases that are being developed to anticipate the implications for society.
• Equity And Opportunity: Public-facing tools need to work well for everyone. A public launch of an AI-enabled tool or program necessarily will impact people from different demographics, ethnicities and geographies. When choosing a tool, ask yourself what existing biases this tool could magnify. What inequities exist in different cohorts and communities, and will all people find the same access and value? More than just considering the tool’s utility, contemplate the longer-term effects of AI deployments that favor some groups over others.
• Environmental Responsibility: Sophisticated AI models that yield differentiating capabilities for your organization can require significant energy during training and testing and as the deployment scales. What does this mean for the organization’s carbon footprint and climate impact? Every enterprise determines its own threshold for environmental responsibility, so with AI, acknowledge and then assess the impact your AI endeavors will have on the planet.
• Truth And Transparency: When hyper-personalized text can be created in an instant with a Large Language Model (LLM), and when realistic images, videos and voices can be created en masse with the power of Generative AI, there is the potential that, at least in the digital realm, the broader society may lose confidence in what is true and real. What is your organization's responsibility in ensuring these tools are developed and used in a way that promotes transparency? If AI tools lead to a society that views technology as a source of fiction and deception, not only does that degrade public trust, it may also severely limit the grand potential of AI.
Public responsibility in business has always been important, but in light of AI, the stakes today are high. The long-term tangential consequences of AI will determine whether this is a technology that fulfills our wildest aspirations or one that is potentially perilous and untrustworthy. To make the right ethical, pro-social choices with AI, take the time to become informed and think through potential societal outcomes. It is possible to do right while doing well, and in the age of AI, leaders have an opportunity to steward this powerful technology toward its most valuable and beneficial use for all.

title: Council Post: Four Steps To Finding Clarity And Taking Agency Over AI
text:
Keynote speaker, author, and leadership coach. Co-Founder and President, Academic Leadership Group. Instructor, Harvard Extension School.
Leaders, do you know where your people are on the use of artificial intelligence (AI)?
During a recent workshop with 50 leaders on the topic of AI, the instructor conducted an informal survey with a show of hands. She asked where each participant was on the AI utilization continuum, from “I’m never going to use it” to “It’s amazing; I’m already using it,” with “undecided” in the middle. Interestingly, 80-90% of the group were undecided on the use of AI, taking a wait-and-see attitude toward it.
It is understandable. We have a lot on our plates these days, with more work to do than hours available to do it, but leaders have the opportunity and responsibility to embrace the possibilities of AI. AI is already rapidly changing work and industry landscapes; it will eventually affect every industry. But many of us aren’t as aware or proactive about it as we should be.
The impact on jobs will be far-reaching. The World Economic Forum’s The Future of Jobs 2020 report estimated that new technologies like AI will disrupt 85 million jobs globally between 2020 and 2025 while creating 97 million new job roles.
Disruption is scary—and it brings opportunity. You have a tremendous opportunity right now to take your employees, yourself and your organization from a feeling of defensiveness or powerlessness to one of clarity and agency. It begins by taking stock and learning how to go beyond standard strategic planning and goal-setting:
1. Gather intelligence.
Do this by talking to your people. You may have read about AI being used to create artwork or write college application essays—along with the criticisms of the results—but it is time to find out if your employees are finding ways to put AI to good use. You may be surprised at how much your staff is already using AI tools. Look to those staff who have embraced AI. How are people using AI? Are they finding ways to allocate basic but necessary tasks to free up time for more important work?
2. Find out for yourself.
The only way to truly understand the capabilities and drawbacks of AI tools is to try them out. For example, my business partner asked her parents—both retired academics—if they’d heard about AI tools like ChatGPT. They had, indeed, and had formed some opinions about them. But neither of them had tried it out. So she opened ChatGPT and invited them to explore. Her mom asked the AI to tell her a story about a three-year-old who picked up a shell on the beach. She was amazed by the beauty and creativity of the tale it spun. This inspired my business partner's dad to test it in his area of expertise, mechanical engineering. And he immediately saw the flaws in the response. It’s this kind of firsthand experience that will give you an understanding of how these tools work and their current limitations, how you may be able to employ them and how they may impact your profession and industry.
3. Get engaged.
Embrace and investigate the questions AI sparks, and do it together with your employees. Many companies have a top-down culture of employees waiting for senior management to approve and introduce new tools. However, every employee should be exploring and engaging with AI tools. Again, start with yourself and be the lead learner so you can be a model for your staff to help them feel supported by you and the organization. Every employee has the opportunity to begin thinking about how they can use their uniquely human capabilities so that rather than trying to compete with or outrun AI tools, they can harness them.
4. Get creative and become purpose-driven.
There is a tendency to be reactionary to new tech. Instead, think about the possibilities and get creative together. Have your team members play with AI tools in groups of six or eight people, asking AI to do something very closely related to their own jobs. Then, come back to debrief them on their thoughts and genuine reactions. Ask: “What made you nervous? What scares you? Can you use it? How do you think AI might change your job, for the better or worse?” Help your team members gain a better sense of purpose by inviting them to now ask themselves: “What do I want more or less of in my work? What kind of work am I doing when I get into a flow state? What is the work that I don’t find fulfilling that I can delegate to an AI tool? What work would I like to do that I don’t yet have the skills to do?”
Everyone wins.
Exercises and questions like these help you and your staff become more comfortable adapting to uncertainty and evolving your professional identities—skills that are an absolute necessity as the future of work will demand constant growth and an ability to pivot as the needs of industries, organizations and individuals change in ways that we've never seen before.
McKinsey has found that “People who find their individual purpose congruent with their jobs tend to get more meaning from their roles, making them more productive and more likely to outperform their peers.”
Gallup estimates that disengaged employees cost their employees the equivalent of 18% of their annual salary. That’s a scary number, given that Gallup also estimates almost two-thirds of U.S. employees are disengaged.
Your most talented people will stay where their sense of purpose aligns well with their jobs and where they feel the company supports their professional and personal development. It’s a win-win for you, your employees and your company.

title: Microsoft's multibillion-dollar investment in OpenAI could face EU merger probe
text:
Microsoft's multibillion-dollar investment in artificial intelligence firm OpenAI could face a full-blown merger investigation in the European Union, EU officials signaled Tuesday.
The European Commission, which is the executive arm of the EU, said that it was embarking on a competition investigation looking at the markets for virtual worlds and generative artificial intelligence.
As part of its assessment, the Commission said that it wants to understand how competitive these markets are currently and gain insight on how competition law can help these fields.
The EU Commission also said it is "looking into some of the agreements that have been concluded between large digital market players and generative AI developers and providers" and singled out the Microsoft-OpenAI tie-up as a particular deal it will be studying.
"The European Commission is checking whether Microsoft's investment in OpenAI might be reviewable under the EU Merger Regulation," the Commission said in a statement on Tuesday.
Microsoft did not immediately respond to a CNBC request for comment.
The Commission said it has sent requests for information to "several large digital players" and is also seeking views from interested parties, which have until March 11 to submit responses.
"Virtual worlds and generative AI are rapidly developing," Vestager said in a statement Tuesday. "It is fundamental that these new markets stay competitive, and that nothing stands in the way of businesses growing and providing the best and most innovative products to consumers."
Microsoft has put billions of dollars into OpenAI, the firm behind the popular AI chatbot ChatGPT. The company has integrated some OpenAI technology into its Office, Bing, and Windows products and provides OpenAI with its own Azure cloud computing tools.
The Redmond, Washington-based technology giant first invested in OpenAI in 2019, contributing $1 billion in cash.
The company then grabbed headlines last year, when it reportedly poured a further $10 billion into OpenAI, with its total investment to date reportedly swelling to $13 billion.
News of the EU review comes after the U.K.'s Competition and Markets Authority announced in December that it was launching an initial review into Microsoft's investment. The U.S. Federal Trade Commission is also reportedly assessing the tie-up, according to Bloomberg News.
The CMA said it is assessing whether Microsoft's stake in AI created a "relevant merger situation," citing "a number of developments in the governance of OpenAI, some of which involved Microsoft" as a primary source of concern.
Earlier in the year, OpenAI faced a period of tumult when its CEO Sam Altman was ousted from the board in a shock move. In a dramatic turn of events, ex-Twitch CEO Emmett Shear briefly took the top job, before being removed and replaced with Altman, while the board was given a makeover.
As part of that refresh, Microsoft added its own observer to sit on the board, leading to concerns that the company may be exerting control over OpenAI. For its part, Microsoft has sought to stressed that its designated board observer, who was recently named Dee Templeton, is a nonvoting member.
At the time of the CMA announcement, Microsoft said that it did not in any way hold equity ownership in OpenAI, while OpenAI said that it remained independent and operates competitively.
"Their non-voting board observer does not provide them with governing authority or control over OpenAI's operations," an OpenAI spokesperson told CNBC via email in December.
"While details of our agreement remain confidential, it is important to note that Microsoft does not own any portion of OpenAI and is simply entitled to share of profit distributions," Frank Shaw, Microsoft Chief Communications Officer, said in a December statement.
At the heart of concerns is Microsoft's close partnership and investment in OpenAI, which gives the Redmond titan access to one of the most advanced developers of AI tools today. OpenAI's GPT-4 large language model can handle a rumored 25,000 words of input text — a big step up from the existing ChatGPT limit of 4,096 characters.
Academics have said that GPT-4 has demonstrated human-level performance in various academic exams, while some AI researchers and technologists have speculated GPT-4 may come close to artificial general intelligence, or AGI, which is meant to be as smart or smarter than humans.
- CNBC's Hayden Field and Kif Leswing contributed to this report

title: Author Post: The Top 5 Technology Challenges Of 2023
text:
Looking back on the past year, I used a combination of feedback from my clients and activity on this blog to determine your biggest technology concerns for 2023.
Since you may have missed some of my postings here, consider this your quick and easy recap of the biggest technology challenges of 2023 and what you can do differently in 2024 to address them successfully.
To keep you reading until the end, these are snippets from my top-ranked blogs in descending order, with the highest-ranking topic covered last.
5. Cloud Partnerships and Contracts
It’s no secret–cloud providers command big money. They want you to move to the cloud at any cost. Even with huge initial discounts, a strategic partnership in which they agree to use your services as part of the deal, or by enabling you to migrate faster, once the consumption starts, you are locked in for years. Cloud providers then have a source of annual recurring revenue, which adds up and makes them extremely profitable.
Challenges for Technology Teams
The fundamental conundrum is that a company agrees to spend millions in the cloud. Still, they may not be aware of the potential costs and impact on their application health and performance if they migrate too quickly to satisfy their minimum spend requirement.
Additionally, there’s the challenge of determining the most suitable cloud provider for their technology investments. Different providers excel in various technologies but may lack maturity in others. A common issue is that companies frequently migrate all their application workloads onto a single cloud provider, which may not always align with their business SLAs or objectives.
At the same time, we cannot know what our business, data, or transactional growth rate will be over the next few years. These variables vastly impact spending in the cloud. We can only estimate the high-level growth for months, not years.
As a result, we cannot predict our costs, what technologies we will need, and, therefore, what the cost of our usage will be. The cloud doesn’t work in round, predictable numbers. This is why these relationships are fraught with risk, complexity, and the unknown.
We see companies not meeting the minimum spend requirement because their estimates were off. This is wasted money. Why are the estimates so off?
Migrations to the cloud generally take longer than expected because the companies don’t have a firm grasp on what it is they are migrating.
Some companies enter into partnerships with cloud providers in which the provider agrees to use the company’s services as a customer in exchange for a better deal on cloud services. These arrangements can be multi-year in nature, locking you into a situation that may not ultimately be in your company’s best interest.
How to Do Better in 2024
Before you consider locking down a three-year commitment or entering into a strategic partnership where the cloud provider will use your services if you agree to spend a certain amount with them yearly, I recommend looking before you leap.
Companies are moving to the cloud without understanding the full consequences–i.e., technology costs–of doing so. They may reason, let’s move there now and figure it out later, but often, it’s too late because the financial damage has already been done. It’s fine to migrate to the cloud, but the move has to be done for the right reasons while taking into account
- The enterprise technology needs
- The costs of supporting application workloads on a consumption-based model
- How to optimize 1% of your resources, which can lead to substantial savings in cloud costs. (My company has seen optimizing the top 1% of processes can yield a savings of 50% in costs.)
Without these safeguards, you are locking yourself into more than you need, wasting money.
Focus on migrating application workloads that will be cost-efficient and can take advantage of native cloud services. Then, over time, focus on the workloads that were not built for the cloud and refactor or rewrite them so they can be migrated with attention to the additional costs they will incur.
In the end, you will have data in three places – the cloud, a data center, and SaaS applications, which are also in the cloud.
For more on cloud partnerships and contracts, read Cloud Partnerships And Multi-year Contracts: Look Before You Leap.
4. Redefining Technology in the Age of AI
No look back on 2023 would be complete without mentioning AI. The explosion in AI growth, exacerbated by the introduction of Chat GPT in November of 2022, is further compounded by the cascading effect of other applications that leverage its abilities to do more, faster, and better.
ChatGPT is estimated to have 180.5 million users globally, out of which 100 million people use the generative software weekly, including 92% of the Fortune 500 companies.
The Challenges for Technology Teams
AI and other services are enabling businesses to build and deploy their tech faster than ever without the help of the technology team on Day 1. But that doesn’t mean we still don’t need to figure out how to support, integrate, and enable these innovations to be part of enterprise technology ecosystems.
Plus, with the explosive adoption of AI, IoT, and business applications, the data creation and growth rate will only increase, and it’s already at levels that are becoming unmanageable for existing technology teams. Companies that want to build their own AI services are going to struggle with acquiring talent. But an even bigger gap will be readying the data to train and support the AI models.
You cannot build an effective AI solution if the data is not clean, available, classified, or known. We need proper data governance, security, and other controls to validate the AI models we are building and deploying to preclude bias and ensure answers are accurate and that the overall system is safe to use.
How to Do Better in 2024
It’s time for a new mindset in response to the AI revolution. With millions of new technology services and applications being brought online over the next several years, things will need to change and rebalance.
Rather than replacing jobs, new jobs will be created due to this rate of change. We will need to invest more in new technologies and create new solutions to manage them that do not exist today.
Step up to the challenge. Your job is likely needed now more than ever, and if it isn’t, there’s probably something else you can do to help make sense of it. Rather than worry about our future in the age of AI, let’s think about how we—businesses and technologists—can work more collaboratively to reap the benefits of one of the greatest technological innovations of the century.
For more on getting a grip on AI realities, read Redefining Technology and Business in the Age of AI.
3. Estimating Budgets for the Cloud
With more cloud spending comes more decisions for CFOs on what budget requests to approve and decline without impacting the pace of innovation or potentially increasing the risk of bringing key technology services offline during critical times. So, it’s no surprise cloud spending remains a quandary for CFOs to estimate.
The Challenge for CFOs
CFOs are responsible for ensuring that technology investments deliver a positive return on investment (ROI). But in the era of cloud spending, the ways CFOs evaluate ROI–and therefore make budget decisions–are changing.
Cloud spending is not predictable, and there is a lack of accuracy when forecasting out for several years. Therefore, the financial models typically used fall short regarding cloud technology.
How to Do Better in 2024
My advice to CFOs is three-fold:
- Claim your rightful seat at the IT table (Collaboration from the start is key.)
- Understand the Total Cost of Ownership for your technology system (These costs compound over time and are often overlooked.)
- Improve the technology and application efficiency (See the next section.)
For more on cloud spending, read CFOs: How Can You Evaluate Budget Requests for Cloud Spending.
2. Improving Technology Efficiency
Incorporating efficiency as a standard measure is a cultural change within technology organizations that needs to take place now for the sake of our cloud bills as well as our sustainability responsibilities. Once you implement a mindset of efficiency within technology, the impact on the bottom and top lines and how you build and deploy all code, processes, and data going forward can be tremendous.
The Challenge for Technology Teams
Historically, technology teams have not been designing with the efficiency of code or processes as a major driver in our application development processes. Companies often accept inefficient code and processes into production without focusing on what it’s going to cost this year and beyond. What if an application costs one thousand dollars to run but only needs to cost one hundred dollars to get the same results?
If the applications are not designed with efficiency or resource consumption in mind, the costs will add up over the 10 or 20 years the application is in production. Another thing that will not go down unless you start putting a focus on efficiency is your carbon footprint. (See the next section.)
How to Do Better in 2024
We need to change this by including efficiency as part of the acceptance criteria for the business. To increase efficiency, we must reduce the resources each application process or code consumes, thereby lessening the burden on the server where everything is running.
Just a seemingly small increase in efficiency can yield huge returns when you consider the negatively compounded nature of inefficient processes and the millions of times that process runs each day.
If you’re not using the capacity, you don’t need it, at least for now. However, we must shift focus to the bigger, long-term capacity plays at hand to impact efficiency. We need to define a measurement standard for efficiency across the industry and over time (FinOps for Data and Code are showing promise for doing just that.)
More efficient systems require fewer resources like CPU, memory, storage, and bandwidth to process the same workload as an inefficient system. The design choices we make in how we design the data model, coding, and processes all have lasting impacts on the bottom line, both from a resource perspective and, more importantly, on the financials, as most applications are used for 10 to 20 years. What is that code’s total cost of ownership (TCO) in the long term, and how can this be influenced during the design process?
For more on efficiency in technology systems, read Why Efficiency Should Be Part of Your Acceptance Criteria.
1. Green Data Centers
I was thrilled to see this topic garner the most views on my blog in 2023 because it is also about efficiency. In fact, everything I write and talk about comes down to efficiency, including my book.
It’s great that companies like Microsoft, AWS, and Google are designing green data centers using 100 percent renewable energy, focusing on the buildings that house our data to try to control emissions. But another less talked about problem is that most applications and systems running in these data centers were not designed with efficiency in mind.
The Challenge for Technology Teams
Software development is not often associated with environmental impact. However, the more CPU applications in use, the greater the carbon footprint and direct impact on the environment. Also, most companies pay for licensing based on the number of CPUs required, so you get a bang for your buck, as well as for sustainability, by focusing on efficiency.
It promotes a false sense of comfort to say the data centers are green, saving energy if the applications themselves are inefficient and wasteful. It’s the equivalent of building a new energy-efficient house and then stocking it full of appliances from the 1980s–you’ve just canceled out your efficiency gains.
How to Do Better in 2024
We can reduce our software’s energy and resource footprint by focusing on writing efficient, optimized code. Here are a few ways to accomplish this:
- Design and promote efficient algorithms and data structures.
- Reduce redundancy of code or repeated operations–Keep it SIMPLE.
- Leverage code profiling and code optimization for the top 1% of processes.
- Develop and implement green coding practices.
To learn more about how to make the shift toward green coding, read How Green Is Your Data Center? Optimize Code To Reduce Greenhouse Gas Emissions.
Another year of the status quo will just promote additional layers of inefficiency. Outdated legacy systems are costing us dearly in terms of system health.
I will continue to talk about these issues, raise flags, and request your feedback to work together toward a mindset shift that replaces the end of abundance in technology with the era of efficiency.

title: Council Post: Five Ways To Get Your Employees AI Ready
text:
Krista Neher is the CEO of Boot Camp Digital, a 6X best-selling author, international speaker & recognized digital marketing thought-leader.
Artificial intelligence (AI) is already important—and it is only becoming more important. It's estimated that 80% of businesses are already using or have plans to use AI. Eighty-six percent of employees want training on AI, and 90% of business leaders say that knowing how to use AI tools like ChatGPT is an important skill.
There is no question that AI is transforming how we work and that it is here to stay. Employers and businesses need to act quickly to get their organizations up to speed to unlock the potential of AI. Over the last year, most of my company's clients have said that AI is a top priority for training for their teams.
If you want to grow the AI skills of your organization, here are five steps you can take now to get started.
1. Establish an AI usage policy.
AI is a powerful tool, but it isn’t without risks and limitations. Organizations and employees need to understand these risks.
AI risks include concerns regarding privacy, security, bias, accuracy, copyright and transparency. Every organization should have a policy that covers these areas. Organizations need to have standards in areas like information-sharing and security.
2. Provide ethical AI training.
Once a policy is established, employees need to be trained on the policy. Employees using AI irresponsibly put an entire organization at risk. Employers should have mandatory training on ethical AI use that mirrors the organizational policy. According to Salesforce, 70% of employers say they don’t believe their employees have the skills to use generative AI effectively or securely.
3. Build organization and department plans.
AI is likely already being used by most of your organization. The problem is that current AI usage at most businesses I work with is ad-hoc. Early adopters use it regularly as they see fit, but there isn’t a plan or strategy for the broader organization.
To unlock the power of AI, organizations and departments need clear strategies and plans on how AI can be used. This provides direction for employees versus an ad-hoc approach.
The organization should develop a clear strategy that is deployed to department heads. Department heads can then create plans for their teams. This allows AI to become strategically embedded into the organization. This will increase the effectiveness of AI since its use will be strategic and focused instead of scattered.
4. Train employees on effective AI use.
AI is accessible and being integrated into more and more tools that business professionals already use. Zoom, Microsoft and Google are all integrating AI into their products. AI is everywhere.
Employees need training on how to use AI effectively. Garbage in causes garbage out. If employees don’t understand how AI works and the mechanics of prompt engineering, they likely won’t get great outputs from AI.
AI prompting requires training and practice. Train employees on creating better prompts to get better results from AI.
5. Set goals and optimize.
You don’t get results if you don’t measure. Measure the uses and impact of AI in your organization. This is the only way to know if you are making an impact.
Set goals and key performance indicators (KPIs) for each stage of your implementation. From policy to employee usage, measure the impact on your organization. AI is still new and changing, so as you get data, be agile and evolve. Optimize your efforts and build plans to share successes and ideas across the organization.
Unlocking the power of AI starts with having and communicating a clear policy to protect your organization. Next, businesses must have a strategic plan for how AI can benefit them. The strategy should clearly define the best uses of AI, and teams should be trained on how to use it. Ultimately, businesses need to measure the impact of their investments. KPIs and measurements should be set to be sure that the benefits of AI are meeting expectations.

title: Council Post: AI Arbitrage Is The Next Frontier Of Value Creation
text:
Now CEO of Ascendion, Karthik has led significant business operations and transformation in software engineering for more than 20 years.
Businesses can unleash innovation as AI “eats” IT services
AI offers technology and business leaders the biggest disruption in the $1.4 trillion IT services industry since the invention of the Internet.
Every technology worker—contact center agents, coders, test engineers, data analysts, IT support and more—will get 20% to 50% more when enhanced by AI bots (freeing up capital to fuel innovation, grow faster, improve agility and improve countless worker and consumer experiences).
Economies of scale, platforms and wage arbitrage have delivered massive amounts of service value since the 1960s, and they will remain relevant, but new-gen AI bots are bringing us to the next inflection point in tech value via AI arbitrage as work gets moved to software.
Oh, and this will take years, not decades.
Disrupting The Trillion-Dollar IT Services Industry Is Good For Business
On November 30, 2022, OpenAI released a free demo version of ChatGPT. In 60 days, it had 100 million users, and viral growth has continued since.
That starting gun set off a mad dash of optimism, opinions, panic and early-stage innovation, signaling a disruption in how value is created in nearly every enterprise. Unless you were around when electricity became common, you’ve never seen anything like this.
Anthropic, Amazon, Microsoft, OpenAI, Google and others have—rightfully—captured our imaginations with developments, opportunities and challenges offered by generative AI.
Yet every leader should recognize a critical truth CIOs already know: GenAI will give you a pancake recipe written in rhymed couplets, but that won’t help your bank or healthcare company unlock value from technology.
Why? Because none of these amazing bots work like magic out of the box at the enterprise level. GenAI doesn’t turbocharge value without being integrated into existing technologies, compliance requirements, data systems and workflows that have often been cobbled together over decades.
Service teams—internal groups and external partners—have to do this work in a way that activates three value levers with a cumulative economic impact (aka savings) that can accelerate innovation and growth.
Economies Of Scale And Expertise: Do quality work better and cheaper at scale.
Wage Arbitrage: Find the right talent at the right cost.
AI Arbitrage: Unleash the true potential of your workforce at a lower cost.
(Estimates are illustrative, but they are based on multiple sources and give a sense of what is coming.)
Five Tactics To Unlock AI Arbitrage
Regardless of whether services come from inside or outside the company, the economics of AI arbitrage change the economics of IT as the generative AI bots “eat” IT services.
The journey won’t happen overnight, but every leader can get started. Here are five no-regrets steps to leverage AI arbitrage.
Demand AI innovation from partners. CIOs should require service partners to stay ahead. That’s their job now. Assess potential partners through questions like "Who is pushing the GenAI envelope? Who can help keep us ahead of the game? Who will help us innovate?" Keep an eye on the future and assess partners today on how credibly they are pushing toward generative AI deployment.
Enhance your people with AI. Taking humans out of processes entirely is immensely difficult (and causes backlash). It might sound seductive (cheaper!), but don’t hold your breath. Instead, identify where AI can give your team superpowers. Elevate customer service reps with intelligent assistants. Augment analysts with data insights. The goal is human-AI collaboration, not automation. Enhance your worker and consumer experiences to get value next quarter (rather than sometime in the next decade.)
Start with software and data. After several years of digital transformation, enterprise software engineering and data management are low-hanging fruit. You likely already have the technical capabilities and contracts to embed AI here first. Quick wins build internal confidence and capabilities before expanding AI more broadly across the business. Yes, ultimately, GenAI will be applied to friction points along every value chain within nearly every company, but to start building GenAI muscles, the best first stop is the office of the CIO.
Measure productivity that matters. “You can see computers everywhere but in the productivity statistics,” wrote Nobel-Prize-winning economist Robert Solow back in 1987. New research from my company Ascendion and HFS Research found that about 85% of early adopter enterprise innovators are (finally) starting to see productivity improvement driven by generative AI! Ensure your GenAI investments impact key performance indicators upfront, then monitor rigorously. If projects aren’t moving the needle on productivity, Cost of Goods Sold, or revenue per employee, go back to the drawing board.
Get your CFO to power GenAI innovation. Internal skunk works projects can be great, but only if they deliver returns. AI-fueled productivity—AI arbitrage—needs to show up in internal financials and partner contracts quarter over quarter, year over year. We look at AI as “an IT thing,” and it is, but finance, procurement and legal also play essential roles in managing risk and return. Transformational CFOs are every bit as important in driving this change as CIOs, CTOs and business line leaders.
Executives taking decisive action to harness AI’s potential will gain a sustained competitive advantage. Laggards risk being left behind. The time to develop your AI strategy is now. Start by following these five moves to lead your organization confidently into the new era of enhanced productivity.

title: Council Post: AI At The Helm: Understanding The Impact Of Copilots And Generative AI On The Digital Modernization Journey
text:
Dr. Ravi Changle, Director - Artificial Intelligence and Emerging Technologies, Compunnel.
In the rapidly evolving digital landscape, the emergence of artificial intelligence (AI) has been a game-changer. As we stand at the cusp of a new era, AI is no longer just a tool; it has become a partner, a copilot, guiding us through the complexities of digital modernization.
The advent of AI copilots and the fascinating realm of generative AI are reshaping how we approach technology, business and even creativity.
The Transformative Role Of AI Copilots In Modern Business And Creativity
AI has undergone a significant transformation in the digital landscape, evolving from a tool for task automation to a collaborative partner. This evolution is driven by advancements in machine learning, natural language processing and predictive analytics, enabling AI copilots to understand and predict human needs, thereby providing adaptive and contextually relevant support.
In business operations, they have become crucial in streamlining processes, enhancing decision-making and predicting market trends, like in supply chain management and project allocation. In customer service, AI copilots like chatbots offer real-time, personalized assistance, improving customer satisfaction and operational efficiency. Moreover, their role in creative fields marks a significant shift, as they assist in areas like graphic design and content creation, enhancing human creativity and democratizing the creative process.
Objectives
The objectives of AI copilots, framed within the contexts of operating, designing, optimizing and troubleshooting, encompass a comprehensive approach to enhancing business processes.
1. Operate: AI copilots aim to streamline daily operations, automating routine tasks and allowing teams to focus on more strategic work.
2. Design: They assist in designing more efficient workflows and systems, integrating AI capabilities into various business functions.
3. Optimize: These tools optimize processes by providing data-driven insights, leading to more informed decision-making and improved efficiency.
4. Troubleshoot: AI copilots aim to identify and troubleshoot issues, offering solutions to complex problems through advanced analytics and machine learning.
AI Copilots: The Vanguard Of Industry-Specific Innovation
AI copilots serve distinct purposes, from improving operational efficiency and decision-making in business to enhancing security and streamlining content creation. Here are a few examples of how AI copilots are transforming industry-specific challenges into opportunities.
Banking, Financial Services And Insurance
In banking, financial services and insurance (BFSI), AI copilots can provide predictive insights for personalized customer experiences and risk assessment, enhancing decision-making and customer engagement.
Healthcare
These AI tools can assist in patient data management, predictive diagnostics and personalized treatment plans. The integration of AI copilots with healthcare systems can help enable faster and more accurate diagnostic models.
Manufacturing
AI copilots can optimize supply chain management, predictive maintenance and quality control. They aid in real-time monitoring and predictive analytics, ensuring efficiency and minimizing downtime.
Pharmaceuticals
The pharmaceutical industry is witnessing a paradigm shift with AI-driven drug discovery and development. AI copilots, for example, can accelerate the research process by analyzing complex datasets, leading to faster and more effective drug development.
Addressing Ethical Challenges In AI Copilot Implementation
Incorporating AI copilots across various industries introduces significant ethical challenges, primarily concerning bias and data privacy. The risk of perpetuating societal biases is heightened if AI copilots are trained on non-representative datasets.
Ensuring data privacy is also crucial, as AI copilots often process sensitive information. The effectiveness of these copilots is contingent upon the quality and diversity of their training data to avoid unfair outcomes. Complying with evolving regulations, such as GDPR, is essential for their ethical and legal use. Moreover, the safety and security of AI copilots are paramount, especially in critical infrastructure, necessitating stringent security measures and regular risk assessments.
Finally, the explainability of AI copilots' decisions is key to building user trust and accountability, requiring a transparent approach to their decision-making processes.
Strategies For Overcoming Challenges In Implementing AI Copilots
To effectively implement AI copilots, a multifaceted approach is required. Developing transparent AI systems is crucial, where explainable AI (XAI) models provide clear insights into decision-making processes. This, coupled with user-friendly interfaces, ensures that AI outputs are understandable and trustworthy. Establishing regular communication channels between AI developers and users boosts transparency and trust, while real-world case studies illustrate practical applications and reinforce the reliability of AI decisions.
Furthermore, comprehensive ethics training for AI developers is essential, covering data privacy, bias prevention and the broader social implications of AI. Hosting workshops and collaborating with ethical bodies ensures adherence to ethical standards and the inclusion of diverse perspectives in AI development.
Addressing security is another critical aspect, requiring robust protocols, regular security audits and continuous employee training in cybersecurity practices. Collaboration with cybersecurity experts ensures that AI systems are safeguarded against emerging threats, establishing a secure and ethical foundation for AI copilots in various applications.
Evaluation Mechanism
Evaluating copilots effectively combines technical and user-centric metrics. Technical aspects like accuracy, response time, scalability, resource usage, learning capacity, robustness and integration ease provide a quantitative measure of the AI's performance.
User satisfaction, efficiency improvement, error reduction, adoption rates and cost savings offer insights into the AI's impact on business processes. Combining these metrics gives a holistic view of the AI copilot's effectiveness, balancing its technical capabilities with real-world business benefits. This comprehensive evaluation ensures the AI copilot not only performs its tasks well but also aligns with the organization's goals and user needs.
Steering The Ship Of Digital Modernization
I believe these copilots are the twin engines driving the ship of digital modernization. When approached strategically using the tips in this article, I believe the impact these copilots can have on digital modernization can be experienced through unprecedented innovation, optimized decision-making and the ability to democratize creativity and hyper-personalize experiences. With a deep understanding of user data, they're curating experiences that are deeply resonant and individualized as we progress on our digital modernization journey.

title: Council Post: How Conversational AI Can Change Sales Training And Processes
text:
Sandy is currently President and cofounder of Industry FinTech Inc, a modern, fully-managed, intelligent back-office platform.
One of the biggest challenges for sales leaders is getting their team to sell like stars. They've tried it all, from classroom training to shadowing on calls and even ready-made email templates. But the results? Often underwhelming. However, AI is transforming the sales landscape, promising to turn sales training and closing deals on its head.
When used strategically, AI can be more than just a tool. It has the ability to offer personalized coaching and real-time feedback, analyze customer interactions, tailor pitches and even predict the best sales strategies.
Per Salesforce's "State of Sales" report in 2022, 37% of high-performing teams claim that AI is radically changing their roles and duties, enhancing their overall efficiency. This article covers the promising AI use cases for sales training and sales as well as challenges in their adoption.
The Power Of Conversational AI In Sales Training
Addressing the 520% increase in manager burnout due to increased workload, conversational AI aims to ensure efficient, unsupervised training with personalized simulations. It also aims to reduce managerial load while boosting team proficiency and confidence. Here are some of the use cases to consider.
Interactive Sales Role-Play
Becoming skilled in sales demands perpetual refinement. This includes honing your pitch, mastering objections and tweaking negotiation skills. Typically, sales managers oversee these trainings, yet their busy schedules might create gaps in the process.
Conversational AI helps replicate real-world sales scenarios through phone calls or virtual meetings. It provides sales professionals with a platform to practice and perfect their skills, backed with immediate feedback.
Knowledge Base And FAQ Assistant
In sales, knowing your product is key, but anticipating every client question is challenging. Imagine a sales rep demoing new software to a big client. On a few detail queries, the rep fumbles, needing tech team backup—often unavailable, leading to potential delays and diminishing client interest.
But in such cases, conversational AI trained on product specifics can help reps get real-time, custom advice. It not only responds but also learns to improve with each interaction.
Personalized Learning Paths
Traditional sales training models are not one-size-fits-all, as they do not always meet the varied needs of sales teams. On the other hand, personalized training through conversational AI analyzes each salesperson's unique skills and gaps, tailoring training for precision impact. By syncing with CRM systems and evaluating real-world client interaction data, this AI pinpoints specific areas of improvement in each individual.
Conversational AI Streamlining Sales Processes
Conversational AI is also changing the way we sell. Gartner, Inc. says that by 2028, 60% of B2B sales will use AI, up from just 5% in 2023. This big change shows how AI helps make sales better and faster. Let's look at how conversational AI is doing this.
Lead Qualification And Scoring
Lead generation is crucial for sales success. Conversational AI helps actively engage with potential customers through website chats and product inquiries, making interactions feel more personal and insightful.
Conversational AI doesn't just track interest; it understands and predicts it. Analyzing past conversations and customer behaviors can identify who is most likely to make a purchase. This means sales teams can focus on leads that are not just interested but ready to buy. The result could mean more efficient and effective sales, with a personal touch provided by conversational AI.
Automated Follow-Ups And Nurturing
Conversational AI automates sales tasks by handling repetitive jobs like follow-up emails and customer inquiries. When integrated into CRMs, it can improve customer support efficiency and expand community outreach.
By leveraging audience personas, this technology enables the generation of highly personalized follow-up messages and emails, helping to foster enduring customer relationships.
Upsell And Cross-Sell
Conversational AI is like a smart sales friend who knows what customers want. It looks at their likes, shopping habits and reactions to ads, giving ideal product suggestions. While making product suggestions, the AI virtual assistant can create upselling and cross-selling opportunities for sellers like skilled salespersons.
Influencing Buyer Decisions
There's also "Emotion AI" in sales now. It listens to how customers talk, watches their faces and understands their tone. This helps salespeople connect better with customers by tailoring their approach to the customer's feelings. It makes conversations more real and can help in making successful deals.
Conversational AI: The Promise And The Challenges
While conversational AI can provide several benefits for both sales training and sales processes, there are challenges to consider regarding the AI itself as well as its adoption.
In sales training, for example, conversational AI demands continuous adjustment to suit various sales styles and industry needs, necessitating regular updates and data training for accuracy. Let's explore a few other challenges and how they can be overcome.
Integrating AI With CRM Systems
Integrating AI with CRM systems might disrupt workflows due to compatibility issues. Involving IT teams early for technical advice and conducting small-scale tests can identify and mitigate integration challenges, facilitating smoother implementation.
Maintaining Data Synchronization
In adopting conversational AI, companies often grapple with data synchronization challenges across systems, leading to information discrepancies. Overcoming this involves employing integrated data management and regular updates, utilizing cloud-based solutions for sync in real-time and establishing a centralized data governance framework for consistent accuracy.
Managing Personal Data With Compliance
Companies adopting conversational AI might struggle with personal data compliance, especially under regulations like GDPR. Overcoming this requires prioritizing data security, maintaining transparent usage policies, keeping systems updated with evolving privacy laws and training staff in data compliance to uphold ethical and legal standards.
These steps require careful planning and a balance between efficiency and ethical data management in AI implementation for sales.
Conversational AI: A Catalyst For Sales And Training Excellence
Incorporating conversational AI into sales functions can help enhance team performance and mirror the abilities of top performers. While it doesn't replace traditional training, it can help boost its effectiveness.
The key is to identify where AI can fill training gaps or improve lead qualification. Optimal AI tools are those that blend into existing workflows, offering robust features, affordability, easy setup and dependable support.
Companies often start with a pilot program to measure AI's impact with minimal operational disruption. Key performance indicators (KPIs) are crucial for assessing AI's role in enhancing onboarding, engagement and sales outcomes with ongoing adjustments made based on these metrics.
