title: Council Post: The Code War: A Mad Race For AI Supremacy
text:
CEO of ReAlpha. Tech entrepreneur: 1 IPO, 2 exits. Author, "Nothing to Nasdaq."
In a world increasingly defined by algorithms and automation, the race for artificial intelligence (AI) dominance has become a breakneck sprint. Nations, corporations and research institutions are pouring resources into developing ever-more sophisticated AI systems, each vying for a coveted edge in this high-stakes competition. This frantic pursuit has been aptly dubbed the "Code War," a battleground where lines between collaboration and competition blur in the relentless pursuit of AI supremacy.
At the forefront of this mad race stand the titans of technology: Google, Amazon, Meta and Microsoft, each wielding vast resources and intellectual capital. These tech giants are not only developing their own AI systems but also acquiring promising startups and talent, further consolidating their hold on the AI landscape.
The size of the generative AI (GenAI) market is already substantial and rapidly growing. In 2023, the market size is estimated to be $44.89 billion, with a projected annual growth rate (CAGR) of 24.40% until 2030. This means the market is expected to reach a staggering $207 billion by the end of the decade.
While the market size of GenAI is currently in the billions, some experts in McKinsey believe it could reach trillions of dollars in the future. This is due to the potential of GenAI to revolutionize entire industries and create entirely new markets.
But the Code War extends beyond the tech giants. Governments, particularly the United States and China, are heavily invested in AI development, recognizing its potential to revolutionize warfare, economic growth and national security. This has led to a geopolitical arms race, with each nation vying for the upper hand in AI technology.
Adding to the drama is the ongoing saga surrounding OpenAI, a non-profit research institute dedicated to the safe development of AI. The mysterious Q-star project, rumored to be an advanced AI with General Intelligence capabilities, sparked controversy and led to the ousting of OpenAI's CEO, Sam Altman. This incident served as a grim reminder of the ethical and philosophical issues surrounding AI development, raising questions about transparency, accountability and the potential for AI to become uncontrollable.
The implications of this mad race are far-reaching. On one hand, the rapid advancement of AI could usher in a new era of prosperity and technological marvels. AI-powered automation could streamline industries, boost productivity and eliminate mundane tasks. AI-driven healthcare could lead to breakthroughs in disease detection and personalized medicine.
However, the potential benefits are overshadowed by a growing sense of unease. Concerns regarding job displacement, the potential misuse of AI for malicious purposes and the ethical implications of AI development are rising to the forefront. The lack of clear regulations and oversight has further fueled anxieties about the potential for AI to exacerbate existing inequalities and undermine human autonomy.
The Code War is not just a technological race, but a battle for the future of humanity. As we navigate this complex landscape, it is crucial to prioritize ethical considerations and ensure that AI development serves the collective good. This can only be achieved through international cooperation, robust regulations and a commitment to transparency and accountability.
Only by approaching the Code War with caution and foresight can we harness the transformative power of AI for the benefit of all.

title: Council Post: Could Artificial Intelligence Help Your Small Business In 2024?
text:
Peter Boolkah (The Transition Guy): award-winning business coach, podcaster & speaker helping high-performing business owners get results.
We can all agree that the majority of small to medium-sized enterprises have had a tough ride over the last three years. The global cost of living crisis, a legacy of the Covid-19 pandemic, has had a profound impact on their supply chains and staffing.
Despite that rather gloomy outlook, entrepreneurship is on the rise. In the U.K., according to government data, there was a 0.8% increase in small businesses forming in 2023. That equates to 46,000 more businesses in the U.K. alone in 2023 than in 2022. This is cause for celebration.
2024: Conquering Continuing Instability
However, while some countries are struggling to get inflation under control and others are perhaps turning a corner, there remains instability in the market, and 2024 is not set to be an easy trading year, certainly at the beginning.
There seems to be an appetite for survival in small businesses, with many pivoting or tapping into markets where they see real need. In all sectors, there are winners and losers, and that is evident now. While retail and hospitality remain under pressure, construction and real estate are also now widely affected. However, there will be businesses within those sectors that outperform others. How are they doing it? That is the question.
Let us return to need. As an entrepreneur, one of your key skills is to identify a need within a customer base that is not currently being catered to, or perhaps is, but with gaps. Entrepreneurs are experts at this. However, then they need to launch, operate and survive in a changed marketplace. How do they do that? Could AI be the answer?
The Role Of AI
Artificial intelligence (AI) is still a controversial tool. We see it used for the greater good—to help police solve a case, for example, or to help doctors make medical advances. It can also be exploited by those with bad intentions and can cause a threat to some.
AI has advanced at a rapid pace over the last few years. It has gone from a tool to help us spell check to now being able to remember databases, which saves us time and money. While some small businesses are jumping on board with AI, seeing it as a way to save money and time, others are more reticent, preferring to stick to more traditional methods.
AI can be used to help small businesses and entrepreneurs in areas such as market research, creating content for marketing campaigns and customer service needs. If you are a small business without the means to employ a large team of people to do these things, AI could give you an edge over your competitors. For example, trawling search engines like Google can be a laborious business, whereas using AI can cut that time in half. Chatbots can be used to help communicate with your customer base when you do not have the budget for a customer service team sitting in the office taking calls.
Final Thoughts
If you are an entrepreneur, AI could provide a way to save money and increase productivity. However, as with all technological advances, you must understand the risks associated. Your customers may not like the idea of communicating with chatbots—they may prefer the personal touch. It depends on the service you are offering and who your customer base is.
I think it is a mistake to dismiss AI as a fad. Get to know what AI is and how it can help you, and then you'll be in a position to make a fully informed decision about whether it may help or hinder your business.

title: Council Post: A Transformation In Scientific Discovery: Why 2024 Will Be The Year Of Specialized AI
text:
Sunil Sanghavi, CEO, NobleAI.
The past year has shown amazing advancements in generative AI. It seemed to be everywhere all at once, from de-aging Harrison Ford to a range of personal and professional pursuits supporting content creation, customer care and even investing.
All these applications were possible because of generative AI systems trained on massive amounts of publicly available data. Of course, these activities also came with their fair share of data ownership concerns, which will surely continue to be negotiated in the months and years to come.
While generative AI may have stolen the spotlight in 2023, another approach to AI—one that applies a very different approach to scientific discovery—has been taking shape behind the scenes. Rather than scrubbing publicly available data, AI in science is more focused. By this, I mean it applies small, carefully curated use-case-specific AI models to help speed scientific discovery.
I believe that this AI has the potential to be a game-changer across a wide range of fields, including medicine, agriculture, engineering and more, which is why I predict 2024 will be the year for specialized AI.
The Slow And Costly Process Of Traditional Scientific Discovery
Until recently, advancements in scientific discovery relied on empirical experimentation, which is almost always cost-prohibitive, time-consuming and limited in scope. That’s why the research into chemical and specialized materials for industrial use has not experienced much innovation in the past 50 years. Researchers continue to be beholden to slow, expensive and data-intensive approaches to discovering new chemical and material formulations.
This is true whether developing improvements to roofing tiles or formulations for cookies. Why? Because developing chemicals and materials is incredibly complex, it often requires experimentation across a multitude of parameters so that researchers can understand the interactions of hundreds or thousands of different ingredients. But now, AI in science is opening the door to a more efficient approach. The goal is to use AI to more rapidly explore a greater range of chemicals and materials in software (before going to the lab) and save potentially months or even years of research and development (R&D) time.
Combining AI With Scientific Principles
Generative AI works by leveraging large amounts of language data (the entire World Wide Web, for example). This method is all about compiling a lot of data to drive learning. The difficulty in using this approach for scientific discovery is that many R&D problems don’t always come with massive datasets. And if researchers use big generic datasets (rather than their own proprietary data or scientifically relevant data) to train their models, the results are often not accurate enough to be useful, lacking any grounding in scientific laws or knowledge.
AI models for specialized scientific discovery work by training smaller, science-based, mostly private data models. I like to call these small science models (SSMs). When you add detailed, industry-specific information to these models, including scientific laws, empirical data, specifications and constraints, you can investigate complex problems faster, even if you’re starting with smaller data sets.
So, how would this work when it comes to a real-world scientific discovery challenge? Let’s consider palm oil as an example. Palm oil is in almost 50% of the packaged products found in supermarkets, everything from snack foods and chocolate to personal care items like shampoo and lipstick. It’s a versatile oil that has a lot of properties that make it useful in a variety of formulations, but the problem is that it’s also a major driver of deforestation.
For companies looking for an alternative that can deliver the same results consistently, science-based AI helps offer a path to discovery that won’t necessarily take years of costly lab time. Instead of starting with a set of inputs to predict an output (which means having access to a lot of data), this AI-enabled method allows researchers to use “inverse design” to start with a desired output. This formulation gives the desired taste or efficacy without palm oil.
When AI is married with scientific principles specifically relevant to complex research, R&D teams can be better positioned to speed discovery while reducing time to market and associated costs—challenges that have traditionally plagued chemical and materials development.
Challenges To Consider
The opportunities presented by science-based AI are also the very features that could pose challenges if incorporation is not done right.
Working with private data requires a strong commitment to data security. Creators of science-based AI models must respect that the data and models are the private property of specific organizations and can’t be shared to build common models.
Science-based AI relies on a sufficient amount of data to fine-tune its discovery capabilities. Each specific task may demand various types of relevant data. However, for numerous organizations, consolidating all pertinent data poses a challenge as it may exist in various formats—some may be digitized in electronic lab notebooks, while others are often found in traditional paper notebooks or other documents. Additionally, certain data might be distributed among different teams. Collecting, organizing and integrating relevant data in a manner suitable for building ML models requires specialized techniques and tools.
The AI models also need to be optimized to manage multiple scientific principles across different scientific disciplines. One formulation might draw on laws and principles connected to biological sciences and also chemistry and even physical sciences. One approach does not fit all cases, and methods should be tuned to the specific needs of the problem.
Have the right team in place that understands how to leverage AI within the total environment. Scientists and chemists may not necessarily be in tune with AI principles, and data scientists are likely not in tune with the depth or science required. What kind of expertise bridges need to be created so these teams can efficiently connect?
A Paradigm Shift In Scientific Discovery
We’re just beginning to hear about some of the most promising uses of science-based AI. Google’s AI firm DeepMind is using AI to identify changes in human DNA that might cause disease. To date, scientists have only classified 2% of DNA mutations as either benign or disease-causing, but DeepMind scientists believe they can increase that percentage to 89% in a mere fraction of the time, dramatically improving the ability of scientists to focus on drug discovery and other disease treatments.
I believe science-based AI will help scientists identify new medicines that won’t spare the malaria-carrying mosquitos that are now evading traditional methods. In the field of energy, it has the promise to identify alternative fuels and technologies while also helping traditional oil and gas companies minimize the impact of fuel extraction. And, like the palm oil example, science-based AI holds great potential for the world of green chemistry, helping scientists replace chemicals, ingredients and materials like polyester, PFAS and certain battery minerals with more sustainable options.
While there’s been a lot of important discussion around its risks and benefits, generative AI, while taking center stage for now, is not the only promising use of AI. I firmly believe there’s reason for a great deal of optimism around what AI can do in the area of scientific discovery.
When applied to specialized challenges, AI holds great potential to have a transformative impact in areas ranging from environmental sustainability to product innovation to human health, and I’m very much looking forward to what 2024 will bring.

title: Council Post: How AI Assistants Will Reshape Corporate Strategy From The Top Down
text:
CEO and co-Founder of AnswerRocket.
The world has watched closely as generative AI tools like ChatGPT have experienced skyrocketing adoption. So far, the focus has mostly been on the way individuals are leveraging the technology for specific purposes. For example, software developers use it to help write code or authors use it to create content.
But AI’s value expands beyond just automating tasks and certain workflows—it can deliver insights to help solve some of the world’s most vexing challenges.
AI Helps Steer Corporations from the Very Top
Running a business in an uncertain economy is as tricky as almost any other endeavor. Business leaders face constant strategic challenges as they look to grow their company, survive volatile market conditions, anticipate changing customer demands, and accommodate complex regulations. That’s why in the future, generative AI use in the enterprise will expand beyond just individuals, teams and departments: There will be AI assistants in corporate boardrooms across the globe, helping companies navigate dynamic markets, increase profits, and gain an advantage over their competitors.
C-level leaders will look to these technologies for guidance as they make the most important business decisions for their enterprise. When these execs are debating issues like whether they should acquire a company, if they should ramp up hiring or which market they should expand to next, there will be an AI assistant in the room that provides analysis and recommendations. AI will have a “seat” at the table, just like CFOs or COOs.
Ultimately, generative AI will influence every important, high-level strategic choice these businesses make. “Influence” is an important word here. If they’re wise and understand the fundamentals of the tech, business leaders won’t give AI assistants carte blanche to steer a company on their own. However these leaders will ask questions that generate rich, data-driven assessments, then weigh their options accordingly. This illustrates the real promise of AI—humans and AI collaborating to produce the best possible outcomes.
High Stakes Require Specialized, Tested AI
Given the stakes, these companies won’t be using general generative AI technologies like ChatGPT or Bard to guide these decisions—they will instead leverage technology that’s been customized for this purpose and for each business. These AI assistants will take into account a company’s industry, its competitors, business goals, historical industry data, etc., to provide executives with the most precise insights possible. AI that is the best at specialization—demonstrating its effectiveness no matter the scenario or contingencies—will win out in the market.
With so much on the line, avoiding hallucinations will be critical. The right choices at the right time can turn a small company into a market leader within a few years. On the other hand, when a business makes just one poor, major strategic decision, it can cost dearly and even lead to bankruptcy. Because of that, these AI modules will have to be finetuned, tested extensively and proven reliable before they’re deployed in the C-suite. This will take some refining, but the tech will be ready within the next 2-3 years.
What Enterprises Can Do To Protect Against Hallucinations
Even as the tech continues to get better and more accurate, enterprises must take proactive measures to ensure they’re getting good insights. First, they need to put in place technical guardrails to prevent hallucinations. Enterprises have to recognize that a large language model is just storytelling—it’s capable of writing fiction and non-fiction. If you want it to tell a fact-based story, you need to provide it with the content it should use to tell that story. Avoid asking for anything outside those bounds and explicitly let the system know that using facts from foundational model training will yield incorrect answers. Then, you must verify that the story generated is factually correct and grounded in vetted data. AI tools can aid users in this verification process by providing precise references to the data and documents used, as well as distinguishing if any facts and figures came from unvetted sources. Interestingly, this is a process similar to what you would do for an outside consultant who is helping with your business.
Human-in-the-loop iterations to create a generative AI business copilot is the other critical component of battling hallucinations. The human broadly serves as a fact checker but also a tone-setter, guardrail enforcer and overall teacher. Their role is to make sure AI is providing relevant, realistic, trustworthy feedback and guidance about the business in a mode that is constructive for the intended use. They don’t need deep technical expertise—they simply need to be a domain expert. For example, the human in the loop overseeing an e-commerce generative AI copilot might be an e-commerce marketing manager—they understand how to evaluate e-commerce performance and can spot a faulty-looking insight immediately. This subject matter expert knows what a good insight looks like and can quickly tell if something looks off. Having these humans in the loop is essential for designing an AI copilot that can converse with users about their business in a way that makes sense to them and that’s tailored to how they think about their business.
Strategic AI Will Determine Market Winners
AI’s biggest value is in the insights it can help uncover. In the corporate world, it’s the strategic decisions that ultimately make the difference between a trillion-dollar market cap or failure. Enterprises are already leveraging AI at the individual and team levels (i.e., in software development, marketing, sales, etc.). The companies that adopt generative AI at the highest level—using AI to guide themselves from the C-suite—will outpace their rivals and thrive for years to come.

title: TikTok becomes first app to cross $10 billion in in-app spending - ET BrandEquity
text:

- 2 min read
TikTok becomes first app to cross $10 billion in in-app spending
Video-streaming platforms like TikTok and Disney+ drove an 11 per cent rise in consumer app sales in 2023, showing resilient demand while the games industry dealt with a double-digit sales decline in China that dragged global sales down by two per cent. TikTok’s in-app purchases of credit that can be used to tip favored creators and live streamers accounted for the bulk of its income and unlocked the secret to monetization on mobile.
ByteDance’s TikTok became the first app to surpass $10 billion in cumulative consumer spending, helping power mobile app sales to a new high in a year revenue from games was down, according to the latest annual report by data.ai.
Video-streaming platforms like TikTok and Disney+ drove an 11% rise in consumer app sales in 2023, showing resilient demand while the games industry dealt with a double-digit sales decline in China that dragged global sales down 2%.
TikTok’s in-app purchases of credit that can be used to tip favored creators and live streamers accounted for the bulk of its income, and “unlocked the secret to monetization on mobile,” according to the market researchers, whose services are used by many of the world’s biggest brands to track the performance of their mobile apps and ads.
“Social apps and the creator economy pioneered new pathways to monetization beyond advertising,” said Lexi Sydow, director of corporate marketing and insights at data.ai. “TikTok laid the groundwork through its content creator tipping mechanism. In 2024, direct consumer monetization in social apps through in-app purchases is set to grow 150% to $1.3 billion as competition ramps up.”
Spending in apps, rather than games, grew as consumers spent more on streaming, user-generated content and dating apps. Still, the bigger revenue driver remained advertising, which rose 8% in 2023 to $362 billion and accounted for two-thirds of mobile sales. That makes the battle to attract and retain user attention paramount, as data.ai estimates 2024 will bring in $402 billion in global mobile ad spending.
Consumers again increased their time spent on smartphones — Indonesia ranked highest with over 6 hours per person per day. The average among the top 10 markets hit 5 hours of daily app usage, and spending in apps increased by 3% in 2023. South Korea, Brazil, Mexico and Turkey all hit 25% growth or more in consumer app spending for the year, according to data.ai.
Chinese budget shopping sensations Shein and PDD Holdings Inc.’s Temu shot up the download rankings, growing by 140%, with Temu leading downloads across 125 markets. Elsewhere, the travel and ticketing sectors staged a rebound in popularity and spending as post-pandemic demand for in-person events and experiences boomed.

title: Council Post: Spy Vs. Spy: In The ChatGPT Era, Who’s On First?
text:
Adam Stern is Founder and CEO of Infinitely Virtual, provider of cloud technology solutions, based in Los Angeles. Twitter: @iv_cloudhosting
Back in the 1960s, when the U.S. faced off against the Soviets, MAD Magazine initiated a snarky proxy war in the form of a recurring comic strip that pitted two animated spies attempting to outsmart each other. In “Spy vs. Spy,” there were no permanent victors.
Fast forward to the ChatGPT generation. In cybersecurity, it’s AI vs AI now, and the black-hatted figure versus the guy in the white hat is no longer as binary as it once was.
Why AI Makes It Difficult For The Good Guys To Respond
Until now, the two sides had been threat actors and security engineers or developers of antivirus software. It was a matter of who’s better at fostering mayhem or defusing the attack. The threat actor came up with something new, and the security vendor asked, “How do we deal with this? How do we prevent damage before threat actors figure it out?”
Today, while more effort is being put into AI, both sides have become increasingly adept at playing offense and defense. Threat actors are using AI to come up with code, while companies like Sentinel-1 and Ironscales (and DNS filtering providers) are deploying AI to their advantage. Even at this early stage, the AI arms race feels less like a stalemate and more like a Sisyphean task. Humans are working in front of a screen 24/7 to try to do something that AI can do within seconds.
What else is new? For one thing, ChatGPT actually learns; it doesn’t rearrange words and call it a day.
Think about it this way: A threat actor can go to a generative AI solution and say, "Write me code that will be undetectable by anti-malware." That code does not exist; it’s brand new. Because it’s never been seen, no website has it. The generative AI solution asks, "What language do you want it in?" The threat actor responds, "Write it in +." Then, it will essentially learn C++ and use its algorithm to figure out the best way to write something brand new—something highly advanced, well beyond the capabilities of previous threat actors in the same time frame.
That’s the "Spy vs. Spy" scenario brought to life.
For example, a KnowBe4 blog, while also citing an article by Eric Geller at The Messenger, recently noted that one of the new ways that AI tools are increasingly being weaponized is by crafting "convincing, highly targeted and sophisticated social engineering attacks." They explain that "most hackers aren’t native English speakers," but they can use AI to "easily produce messages in perfect English, devoid of the basic mistakes Americans are increasingly trained to spot."
"In addition to assisting in social engineering attacks," KnowBe4 also notes, "AI can be abused to write malware or help plan cyberattacks."
One particularly nefarious concern is that by using generative AI, threat actors can develop mutating malware in real-time—that is, malware that mutates every time it generates, making it difficult for current cybersecurity solutions to detect.
Conclusion
Even if these threats are “imperfect,” they are nonetheless challenging to defend against and may fool most of the people most of the time.
Anecdotally, people often perceive the fakes to be more real than real, which ironically suggests that even as threat hunting becomes ever more automated, the need for human intervention has just increased—perhaps exponentially. Think of it this way: Unlike people, the new-era code lacks a conscience.
At least we’ve been warned.

title: Artificial Intelligence Electricity Use Is In The Crosshairs
text:
Artificial intelligence has progressed from sci-fi fantasy to mainstream reality. AI now powers online tools from search engines to voice assistants and it is used in everything from medical imaging analysis to autonomous vehicles. But the advance of AI will soon collide with another pressing issue: energy consumption.
Much like cryptocurrencies today, AI risks becoming a target for criticism and regulation based on its high electricity appetite. Partisans are forming into camps, with AI optimists extolling continued progress through more compute power, while pessimists are beginning to portray AI power usage as wasteful and even dangerous. Attacks echo those leveled at crypto mining in recent years. Undoubtedly, there will be further efforts to choke off AI innovation by cutting its energy supply.
The pessimists raise some valid points. Developing ever-more capable AI does require vast computing resources. For example, the amount of compute used to train OpenAI’s ChatGPT-3 reportedly equaled 800 petaflops of processing power—on par with the 20 most powerful supercomputers in the world combined. Similarly, ChatGPT receives somewhere on the order of hundreds of millions of queries each day. Estimates suggest that the electricity required to respond to all these queries might be around 1 GWh daily, enough to power the daily energy consumption of about 33,000 U.S. households. Demand is expected to further increase in the future.
In a sense none of this is new. Almost since the dawn of the internet, there have been concerns about energy consumption. As the network of servers, data centers, and connected devices has expanded, so too has electricity demand. Conservationists have long pointed out that the continuous operation of these energy-intensive facilities and apparatuses, necessary for maintaining the 24/7 availability of online services, leads to environmental impacts.
Just as with cryptocurrencies and the early internet, AI’s energy consumption may seem shocking without proper context. Critics will inevitably cast the meteoric growth in AI compute as excessive, unnecessary and risky. However, if AI makes workers more productive by, for example, saving programmers time writing code, researchers time finding and reading articles, and ordinary office employees effort engaging in repetitive tasks and document writing, AI will invariably save a lot of energy as well.
Furthermore, these energy savings don’t take account of other direct benefits of AI. Although not the only factor, adding compute enhances AI capabilities from natural language processing to computer vision. While just throwing compute at problems doesn't guarantee progress, it does reliably provide meaningful improvements. Compute serves as the fuel for AI innovation.
Unfortunately, just as with crypto mining, nuances get lost as the different factions square off in the public arena. These debates can quickly turn emotional. With climate change concerns prominent, restrictions on electricity usage are likely to gain momentum as a tactic employed by activists to oppose disfavored industries. Think “Operation Choke Point” for power usage.
We've already seen officials target sectors they deem objectionable by pressuring the banks and payment networks that provide them with financial services. Industries like firearms dealers, payday lenders, and fossil fuel companies have become targets. Despite any evidence of illegality, these industries face pressure from politicians and activists seeking to change their behavior by cutting them off from mainstream financial institutions.
Now with some questioning whether AI development should be curtailed, analogous pressure campaigns in the context of AI compute seem inevitable. Just as banks are being coerced to restrict counter-parties for political reasons, power companies may soon face similar pressure with respect to their most energy-intensive customers.
While activists’ fears aren’t entirely unfounded—there are real risks from AI that need to be considered and addressed—blanket restrictions on electricity use are the wrong approach. Basing power usage rights on political favorability puts us on a slippery slope. For all that divides Americans lately, access to electricity remains thankfully uncontroversial.
Rather than pick winners and losers, policy makers should aim to provide reliable and affordable electricity to all law-abiding, bill-paying customers. Industries like cryptocurrency and AI will naturally improve energy efficiency over time, given this is already a priority within these industries. They should be given they space they need to mature.
We shouldn’t fall for attempts to choke off emerging technologies’ electricity supply just because some industries happen to have gotten caught up in today’s politics. With smart innovation-friendly policy, meeting our energy needs and environmental goals can go hand-in-hand.

title: Council Post: How Alternative Finance Companies Can Use AI To Help Streamline SME Lending
text:
Mantvydas Štareika, CEO at CapitalBox.
Alternative finance couldn’t have taken on lending for small- and medium-sized enterprises any sooner. By the time the financial technology industry had grown enough that alt-finance companies had the capital and ability to start lending at scale, the SME world was more than ready to borrow.
I believe the funding gap that’s plagued SMEs for years is proof of that in and of itself. This long-standing funding gap has its roots in the simple mathematics and zero-sum game of the traditional lending environment. Big banks typically preferred to lend to established businesses with sufficient collateral, avoiding risk whenever possible. SMEs and startups are risky investments, particularly if the sphere is still untested in terms of economic resilience.
While the growth and evolution of European startups over the past 20 years might have changed this perception somewhat, many SMEs still rely on angel investors for funding. But, that option can be risky. When big banks do dispense loans, I've found that they tend to be on the smaller side, and some institutions rely on outdated business models.
As a result, an alt-finance ecosystem has sprung up to meet SMEs’ lending needs. The proof is in the pudding, which is to say the continued growth of this alt-finance ecosystem itself demonstrates the viability of funding SMEs overlooked by many traditional banks. Through my time leading a fintech lending company for SMEs, I've found that, because they aren't major financial institutions, SME lenders in the alt-finance world are often among the first to try out new strategies and technologies related to lending.
Exploring AI In Alt-Finance
No technical innovation has made more of a splash in the past year than the rapid advances surrounding artificial intelligence. These advances have been multifaceted. In addition to technological improvements, AI is also demonstrating broad commercial viability as it becomes available (and even legible) to non-tech-focused businesses and ordinary people.
So it’s not altogether surprising that some alt-finance companies focused on lending have not only adopted AI but are also reaping its benefits. Among the benefits in question is a faster application and approval process. AI can be used to quickly screen loan applications, cutting down on analysis time and flagging only areas that need to be reviewed by a real person. This helps ensure loans are provided as quickly as possible to SMEs, which matters immensely to businesses with much shorter financial runways than your average corporations.
Beyond speeding up the application and loan distribution process, AI can also be used for the criteria some SME lenders consider. For example, at my company, rather than looking at simple collateral in the form of property or financial data like credit scores, we are incorporating new criteria into the application process, such as projected revenue, investor interest and market potential. These factors can all come into play on an application and can balance out an average credit score.
Other companies even take into account things like social reach, which I think makes sense at this point in the global social media and social marketing ecosystem. These lenders aren’t putting on blinders when it comes to evaluating what you might call "non-traditional value."
Considerations When Using AI In Lending
Lenders can train AI on new criteria to see what sticks, what doesn’t and where it all leads. Incorporating AI can help take some of the guesswork out of the whole operation. While it can’t eliminate the inherent trial-and-error processes within this strategy, I've found it can compile and evaluate the data those trials create in a productive way. Humans come up with new criteria, and AI helps put it to the test.
Working with AI is not without its pitfalls, however. We’re already seeing lending-focused AI systems mimic real-world racial biases. Besides ethical considerations and losing the so-called human touch that customers appreciate, AI also brings with it new challenges concerning data privacy compliance.
That being said, however, I nevertheless believe these challenges can be met, and alt-finance lenders are well-suited to address the biases that can emerge within AI-assisted lending. As I see it, alt-finance lenders working specifically with SMEs already have an ideal data set to train AI and smaller customer bases mean a greater ability to monitor biases emerging within the AI systems.
Combine all this with AI’s ability to help evaluate applications, and I believe alt-finance companies could drive a paradigm shift for SME lending. From my view, the capital is there, the criteria are expanding and the willingness to lend is improving. Innovation on all fronts, including AI, has made that possible, and it’s going to influence the future of lending. Rising to the occasion requires working smarter, not harder. Alt-finance lenders using AI must monitor and implement the technology's integration with extreme attention to detail and lots of tiny modifications as they go. The results will be massive.

title: Council Post: Business Leaders—Here's Your Strategic AI Roadmap For 2024
text:
CEO at Planview, a global leader in Portfolio and Value Stream Management.
Years ago, Roy Amara, a cofounder of the Institute for the Future in Palo Alto, highlighted what's now called Amara's Law:
"We tend to overestimate the effect of a technology in the short run and underestimate the effect in the long run."
Today, AI is proving this law true on both ends. Everyday technology is evolving, especially with generative AI challenging our expectations. In the past year, we've seen significant progress, from basic chatbots to GPT-4 passing the bar exam.
The blend of increased intelligence, automation and accelerated productivity is boosting work efficiency to new heights, marking a new era of innovation. To seize this opportunity, leaders need a proactive, forward-thinking approach. With AI advancing rapidly, organizations can no longer afford a passive stance. Prioritizing AI readiness and scalability aligns innovation with business outcomes, providing a competitive edge in the market.
For business leaders, here's a practical roadmap for effective AI adoption in 2024.
Leading AI adopters will leverage data curation.
Winning organizations will curate their data into shared bodies of knowledge that enable AI models like GPT-backed Copilots to drive digitalization at scale.
A recent Gartner report found that nearly 70% of CFOs believe digital spending is underperforming against expected outcomes. The root cause is a disconnect between those outcomes and an organization’s capacity to deliver them. Planview’s Project to Product 2023 State of the Industry Report found that business leaders believe IT teams in charge of digital transformation efforts can deliver 10 times more than their actual capacity. Only 8% of IT and software development plans are ultimately executed.
The major roadblock stems from disparate data. Most organizations leverage myriad different systems and tools to deliver transformation at scale. Fit-for-purpose systems to deliver work are OK in this regard, as standardization isn’t practical. However, none of the different systems are integrated or aligned, and value streams with minimal interoperability cause bottlenecks that hinder transformation efforts from succeeding.
Curating datasets into a common ontology and in a centralized data platform creates a holistic picture of how the business and initiatives are performing. Once that is in place, organizations can then engineer prompts to train generative AI to produce impactful prescriptive insights, identify high-risk initiatives and refine resource allocations. This helps remove drudgery from strategic planning-to-execution processes with AI-powered productivity.
Organizations that unlock this accelerated time to value in 2024 will develop agility to adapt to evolving environments in a much more rapid way.
Copilots will democratize complex enterprise software and uplevel productivity.
Copilots will become fixtures of digital-centric work environments. "Copilot" is quickly becoming less of a proprietary name and more of a staple term for augmenting human performance.
There are a few ways to incorporate Copilots in your organization. Coding Copilots will continue to gain broad adoption in 2024, enabling better code productivity and quality. We will also see increased adoption of application Copilots that democratize technical processes—helping casual, infrequent or novice users maximize the value.
Top-performing Copilots deliver actionable recommendations derived from meticulously curated data. Success in digital initiatives hinges on cross-business alignment, establishing outcome baselines and setting targets while diligently tracking actuals.
Last month, Microsoft announced the availability of its new Copilot, which integrates with M365 applications. My organization launched our Copilot in September, which enables users to maximize the value of our platform through data-driven insights. GitHub also has a Copilot, as does Salesforce and several other leading technology companies.
Review the different Copilot applications and see how each can add value to your business. As stated in this August 2023 Gartner report, enterprise leaders should apply this emerging technology to planning efforts to ensure the formulation of a well-informed digital business strategy.
AI adoption will drive demand for high-level strategy reskilling.
It’s no secret that the ongoing AI hype is sparking valid concerns about its potential to replace human workers across industries. However, in the context of digital transformation, we shouldn’t think about the future with a narrow "human or machine" mindset. It’s really about humans plus machines. Applying AI to augment manual workflows is what will deliver the greatest impact.
Forrester estimates that enterprise AI initiatives will free up to 50% more time in 2024 for IT employees to engage in creative problem-solving, drive customer-centric innovation and generate business value (pg. 4). As AI adoption accelerates, reskilling will be critical to preparing employees for a not-so-distant future when high-level strategic ideation is increasingly fundamental to their roles.
A recent IBM study found that 40% of workers will need to reskill over the next three years due to AI, while early tech adopters who successfully reskill to adapt to AI-driven job changes will report a revenue growth rate premium of 15% on average (pg. 7). It’s important to take steps to identify which internal positions and/or departments will have the greatest need for reskilling, and then start scaling investments accordingly.
Seize the AI advantage.he trajectory from Amara's insightful observation to the current breakthroughs in AI paints a compelling picture of accelerated progress. As we leap from basic chatbots to GPT-4's extraordinary capabilities, the landscape of possibilities is endless.
The curation of data, the integration of Copilots and the strategic reskilling of talent emerge as pivotal strategies for organizations to not only adapt but thrive in this transformative era. The play is clear: Embracing and harnessing the potential of AI positions business leaders to lead in innovation and secure a competitive advantage in the dynamic market landscape ahead.

title: GenAI Assisted Fan Fiction: A Creative Renaissance Or Extinction Event
text:
The advent of Generative AI (GenAI) in the realm of creative writing, particularly in fan fiction, has opened Pandora's box of both opportunities and challenges. While GenAI presents remarkable tools for creativity, its use in fan fiction raises significant concerns, especially around intellectual property (IP) rights, authenticity, and ethical implications.
Opportunity #1: Enhancing Creative Output
GenAI tools have the unique ability to augment a writer’s creative process by assisting in generating ideas, characters, and plot twists that might not immediately occur to the writer. This technology can inspire authors, helping them overcome writer’s block and expand their storytelling horizons. In a recent Harry Potter fan fiction project, a writer used GenAI to generate alternative story arcs for secondary characters, resulting in a richly layered narrative that resonated with the fan community.
Challenge #1: Dependence on AI and Diminishing Creative Skills
Relying heavily on GenAI for content creation could lead to a decline in the creative writing skills of fan fiction authors. Over dependence on technology might stifle individual creativity and reduce the quality of storytelling. A recent survey among a fan fiction community revealed that writers who frequently used GenAI tools felt less confident in their ability to create original content without AI assistance. So, this impact is already being felt.
Opportunity #2: Mimicking Writing Styles
For most fan faction authors, not writing in their personal style is a major challenge. Thus, one of the most intriguing benefits of GenAI is its capability to mimic various writing styles. This is particularly advantageous in fan fiction, where maintaining the tone and style of the original work is crucial. Consider, a fan fiction author used GenAI to adopt J.R.R. Tolkien’s descriptive style in their Lord of the Rings spin-off, seamlessly blending their story with Tolkien’s world, much to the delight of the fandom.
Challenge #2: Intellectual Property and Copyright Infringement
A major concern with using GenAI for fan fiction is the potential violation of intellectual property rights. GenAI algorithms often learn from vast datasets that include copyrighted materials, which they can then inadvertently replicate in new creations. Recently, a fan fiction writer used GenAI to generate a story in the Harry Potter universe. However, the resulting work closely mimicked J.K. Rowling's style and included significant plot elements from the original series, leading to copyright claims from the publisher.
Opportunity #3: Time Efficiency and Productivity
GenAI significantly reduces the time and effort required to produce substantial works of fan fiction. It can rapidly generate drafts, dialogue, and descriptive passages, allowing writers to focus more on refining the story and less on initial content generation. Imagine an aspiring writer, balancing a full-time job, using GenAI to draft chapters of their Star Wars fan fiction quickly, enabling them to complete the story in a fraction of the time it would have taken otherwise while limiting disruption to their professional and personal time.
Challenge 3: Quality Control and Curation Challenges
With the ease of content generation provided by GenAI, there is a risk of an overwhelming influx of low-quality or irrelevant fan fiction. This can make it challenging for communities to curate and maintain high standards of content. For example, a fan fiction platform experienced a surge in AI-generated submissions, many of which lacked depth and coherence, leading to a decline in overall content quality and reader engagement.
Opportunity #4: Collaboration and Community Engagement
We have seen AI systems, in general, help us be more human. GenAI is no different as it can foster a sense of collaboration within the fan fiction community. Writers can use AI-generated prompts and ideas as a starting point for community-driven stories, enhancing engagement and participation. Take for example a Doctor Who fan fiction forum. Members used GenAI to create a series of prompts, around which the community collaboratively built a multi-author story arc.
Challenge #4: Loss of Authentic Voice and Originality
Fan fiction thrives on the unique voices and perspectives of individual fans. GenAI, while capable of generating content, may homogenize these unique voices, leading to a loss of the originality and personal touch that defines fan fiction. For example, in a Star Trek fan fiction community, several members used the same GenAI tool, resulting in stories with strikingly similar narratives and styles, thereby diminishing the diversity and richness of the fan-created content.
Opportunity #5: Language and Accessibility
For non-native English speakers or those with disabilities, GenAI can be an invaluable tool. It can assist in language translation and provide accessible writing aids, making fan fiction creation more inclusive. For instance, a French-speaking fan used GenAI to translate and adapt their Game of Thrones fan fiction into English, effectively reaching a wider audience and receiving acclaim for their work.
Challenge #5: Legal Gray Areas and Ambiguity
The use of GenAI in fan fiction often falls into legal gray areas, particularly concerning derivative works and fair use. This ambiguity can lead to legal challenges and confusion among writers regarding what is permissible. Recently, a fan fiction author faced legal challenges after publishing a GenAI assisted story based on the "Lord of the Rings" series, raising questions about the extent to which AI-generated derivative works fall under fair use.
Opportunity #6: Exploring New Genres and Crossovers
Creating meaningful art requires experimentation, and GenAI enables writers to experiment with a multitude of genres and crossover elements that they might not have time to examine or possibly didn’t even consider. As a result, authors can easily and quickly try a variety of approaches for their work. This can lead to unique and innovative fan fiction pieces that push the boundaries of traditional fan narratives. For instance, a fan fiction author used GenAI to blend elements of science fiction into a classic Pride and Prejudice story, creating an intriguing crossover that gained popularity for its originality.
Challenge #6: Ethical Implications of Deepfakes and Misrepresentation
GenAI raises ethical questions, particularly regarding the creation of deepfakes or content that misrepresents the original characters or authors. This can lead to misleading representations that might harm the reputation of the original works or their creators. For instance, an AI-generated fan fiction piece misrepresented the intentions of George R.R. Martin's characters from "Game of Thrones," leading to confusion among fans and a public clarification from Martin himself.
Opportunity #7: Educational Tool for Aspiring Writers
Writing is more complex than the average person realizes, so even fan fiction authors benefit from a mentor. Thus, GenAI serves as an excellent educational tool for new writers. It can provide guidance on story structure, character development, and dialogue, helping novice writers learn and grow in their craft. For instance, a high school writing club used GenAI to help students develop their skills in crafting fan fiction, resulting in several students winning awards in a national fan fiction writing competition.
Challenge #7: Moral and Creative Ownership Questions
While it can be a powerful educational tool, the use of GenAI in fan fiction also raises questions about moral and creative ownership. Determining the true authorship of AI-assisted works can be complex, especially when multiple parties contribute to the final output. Consider a collaborative fan fiction project using GenAI. It led to a dispute among contributors over the ownership and credit for the final work, highlighting the complexities of authorship in the context of AI collaboration.
Opportunity #8: Preserving and Continuing Legacy Stories
Organizations like Microsoft are using AI to preserve cultural heritage. Similarly, GenAI can be used to continue stories from franchises that have ended or from authors who are no longer able to write. This allows fans to keep enjoying new content in their favorite universes. Imagine after the conclusion of a popular fantasy series, fans used GenAI to create new adventures, keeping the spirit of the series alive and engaging the community in ongoing storytelling.
Challenge #8: Impact on Author and Fan Community Dynamics
The introduction of GenAI in fan fiction is altering the dynamics between original authors and fan communities. While some authors embrace fan fiction creations, others might view AI-generated works as a threat to their creative control and intellectual property. Already, we have incidents occurring where authors publicly criticize the use of GenAI in creating fan fiction based on their work, arguing that it undermines the integrity of the original narrative. Moreover, several authors like John Grisham and George R.R. Marting are suing OpenAI to protect their work.
Whether it’s expanding beloved universes, exploring uncharted narrative territories, or simply making writing more accessible to a diverse range of authors, GenAI is redefining the boundaries of fan fiction and represents a significant leap forward in the creative process. It not only enhances the efficiency and quality of writing but also democratizes the art of storytelling, making it more accessible and inclusive. By providing new perspectives, mimicking various styles, and fostering community collaboration, GenAI is not just a tool but a catalyst for innovation in the realm of fan fiction.
It is also fraught with challenges and ethical dilemmas. From intellectual property concerns to the potential loss of authentic creative expression, the implications are vast and complex. As we navigate this new terrain, it's crucial for writers, legal experts, and the fan fiction community to engage in ongoing dialogue and establish clear guidelines and ethical standards.
Balancing the innovative potential of GenAI with respect for intellectual property and the preservation of individual creativity will be key to harnessing this technology responsibly in the creative arts.

title: What Is An AI PC? Should You Buy One In 2024? Here’s The CES Verdict
text:
You’re going to be hearing an awful lot about AI PCs this year, if CES 2024 is anything to go by. Chipmakers Intel and AMD, as well as all the major PC makers, are pushing the AI PC concept hard. But what is an AI PC and is it worth investing in one at this early stage? Let’s dig deeper.
What Is An AI PC?
A so-called AI PC will contain one of the newly launched processors from Intel or AMD that includes something called a neural processing unit (NPU).
Until now, most AI workloads have been handled by the graphics processing unit (GPU), which are the chips primarily designed to handle graphics and gaming. However new processor ranges such as Intel’s Core Ultra or AMD’s Ryzen 8000G include an NPU to take on the bulk of the AI workloads.
“The GPU is currently the fastest AI processing unit,” AMD’s senior processor technical marketing manager, Donny Woligroski, told me at a CES 2024 briefing. “You’re going to see that performance cross over, with the NPU doing the same levels of [AI] performance as the GPU.”
New laptop and desktop PC ranges from companies such as Lenovo, Dell and HP will be branded an “AI PC” if they include one of these new processors with an NPU.
You may also notice a new key on the keyboard of these PCs. Selected Windows 11 laptops are now shipping with a Windows Copilot key, to the right of the ALT key. This provides a shortcut to the Windows Copilot AI that has been built into Windows 11.
This is hardly the greatest technological innovation of the modern age—you could already access Copilot using the Windows Key + C shortcut combo. But it will make Microsoft’s AI assistant even harder to ignore.
What Will An AI PC Do?
This is the 64-million-dollar question because, frankly, even the PC makers are struggling to formulate clear answers on what these machines will be capable of.
In the short term, you might see AI PCs starting to handle AI tasks locally instead of relying on cloud services such as ChatGPT and Midjourney. In a demonstration at CES 2024 earlier this week, Lenovo showed me a prototype of its forthcoming AI PC service where the AI assistant could help you access features on your PC (ie. “Put my laptop into battery-saving mode”) or answer questions about how much memory the PC has.
Lenovo’s assistant will also perform tasks such as summarizing long documents or writing replies to emails. This can all be done without relying on cloud services, meaning you’ll still be able to use the AI tools even without an internet connection.
That might not be a massive deal for consumers—how many times do you use a PC without an internet connection these days? However, it could be a bigger deal for businesses, who can run AI services locally, without the security fears of sending sensitive information to cloud AI services.
However, when it comes to the bigger picture of what these AI PCs will do that we can’t already get from cloud AI services, the answers start to get wooly.
At an Intel press conference here at CES, top executives from Dell, Lenovo and HP were asked what their AI PCs will do for buyers, and their answers were long on hyperbole, but short on concrete benefits.
“The PC you’ve known before is going to be radically different,” said Sam Burd, president of Dell's Client Solutions Group. “The PC is the productivity tool and AI is a great reason to refresh.”
“This will be a computing revolution,” agreed HP’s president of personal computing, Alex Cho, but he too failed to provide clear examples of what an AI PC will be capable of either.
In fairness to the PC makers, it may be because they simply don’t know. PCs fitted with NPUs have only been on the market for a matter of weeks and it will take time for developers to exploit their capabilities.
“What you’re doing on an AI PC in 2024 is going to be radically different to 2026,” said Intel’s executive vice president for client computing, Michelle Johnston Holthaus.
AMD’s Donny Woligroski agrees. “It will probably be the end of 2025 before you really start to see what an AI PC is capable of,” he told me.
AI and Windows 12
The success or otherwise of AI PCs may hinge on the AI features Microsoft chooses to incorporate in the next version of Windows.
Microsoft and PC vendors have dropped heavy hints that Windows 12 will launch later this year, with an expected focus on AI. The current iteration of Windows Copilot in Windows 11 has got nowhere near the capabilities that Microsoft initially promised, but building a new OS with AI built in from the start gives Microsoft a chance to make amends. And put clear water between Windows and macOS, which has yet to embrace AI in any meaningful way.
Speaking at Intel’s event, Microsoft’s Pavan Davuluri, corporate vice president for Windows and devices, said the company is “thinking about how we rebuild the OS to take advantage of these AI capabilities,” suggesting that more of the AI may run locally on the NPU, rather than running everything in the cloud.
AMD’s Woligroski said he too believed that Microsoft would be “heavily betting” on the Copilot capabilities in Windows 12, with the company “taking advantage of the NPU” wherever possible.
Should You Buy An AI PC Now?
With so much uncertainty about what an AI PC will actually be capable of doing, and with a new version of Windows almost certain to arrive in 2024, it would seem premature to buy a new PC purely on the strength of its AI capabilites at this time. It would make more sense to wait for Windows 12 (likely to be released in the second half of this year) and give developers a chance to start exploiting the new AI chips first.
However, if you need to buy a new PC for other reasons, it certainly makes sense to future-proof yourself by buying an AI PC with that all-important NPU included. Everyday software is likely to take advantage of that NPU in one form or another, even if it’s doing something as simple as blurring the background on video calls or filtering out background noise on audio recordings. Windows 12 may even make an NPU a requirement.
Even if you won’t use the AI services today, you never know what might emerge in the future.

title: Video Game Voice Actors Criticize SAG-AFTRA Over Agreement With AI Company
text:
Topline
Voice actors are taking to social media to criticize SAG-AFTRA, the union representing actors and other entertainment professionals, for an agreement it struck Tuesday with an artificial intelligence company that would allow video game developers to use digital replicas of actors’ voices.
Key Facts
SAG-AFTRA announced Tuesday it signed a deal with Replica Studios, an artificial intelligence voice technology company, for the licensing of actors’ voices for use in video games.
The union stated the agreement will “enable Replica to engage SAG-AFTRA members under a fair, ethical agreement” to create and use a digital replica of actors’ voices for video game development and other interactive media projects.
The union said the agreement will ensure performer consent and negotiation for the use of their voices and will provide performers the ability to opt out of the use of their voice in new works.
SAG-AFTRA President Fran Drescher said the agreement is “a great example of AI being done right,” though the use of AI at all has remained controversial among both screen and voice actors.
SAG-AFTRA stated the deal was “approved by affected members of the union’s voiceover performer community”—but many voice actors posted grievances on X, claiming they weren’t informed of, and did not agree to, the deal and opposed the potential use of AI to replicate their voices.
Chief Critics
Voice actor Steve Blum, known for roles in “Cowboy Bebop,” “Mortal Kombat” and “God of War,” responded to the union’s X post about the agreement, stating: “Nobody in our community approved this that I know of. Games are the bulk of my livelihood and have been for years. Who are you referring to?” Greg Baldwin, a voice actor from “Avatar: The Last Airbender,” said the union “betrayed” voice actors in an X post, adding he would refuse to sign his own “pink slip.” Samantha A. Morrison, a voice acting casting director, accused the union of “straight up spreading lies” over its claim the agreement was approved by voice performers. “No voice actor would willingly approve this. AI has no place in voiceover, or the arts in general!” Morrison posted on X. Veronica Taylor, whose voice credits include Ash Ketchum in the “Pokémon” anime and Cosmos in the “Final Fantasy” video game franchise, questioned how the agreement passed without notice or a vote among SAG-AFTRA members, stating: “Every job brings a unique opportunity for an actor to …act. Encouraging/allowing AI replacement is a slippery slope downward.”
Key Background
SAG-AFTRA has reportedly been locked in negotiations with major video game companies since 2022, largely concerning compensation for voice actors and protections over the use of artificial intelligence. In September 2023, 98.32% of SAG-AFTRA members voted in favor of authorizing a strike against 10 video game companies, though a work stoppage has not yet occurred since the vote. At the time, SAG-AFTRA’s chief negotiator Duncan Crabtree-Ireland said the game companies were not “willing to meaningfully engage” after five rounds of negotiations and threatened a strike.
Crucial Quote
“At this point, I can’t tell what drives your actions more: direct malice, shortsighted greed, or sheer incompetence. Regardless, you’ve failed us yet again, @sagaftra,” Damien Haas, a voice actor known for roles in “Fortnite” and “Halo,” posted on X.
Tangent
The core issues concerning the voice actors’ negotiations with video game studios mirror the negotiations between screen actors and major Hollywood studios, which resulted in a nearly four-month strike that concluded in November. The strike, which overlapped with a writers strike and halted many film and television productions, ended when SAG-AFTRA secured a contract that reformed residual payments and established protections for the use of AI in film. But some actors felt the AI protections didn’t go far enough, criticizing a clause that allows studios to use nonhuman “synthetic performers.” Actress Justine Bateman, who advised the SAG-AFTRA negotiation committee on AI, expressed concerns over potential loopholes in the contract, including an exception for studios to use an actor’s digital double without consent when the project is “comment, criticism, scholarship, satire or parody, a docudrama, or historical or biographical work.” Drescher condemned opponents to the contract as “naysayers who have exploited this momentum of ours.”

SAG-AFTRA and Replica Studios Introduce Groundbreaking AI Voice Agreement at CES (SAG-AFTRA)
SAG-AFTRA Members Vote in Favor of Video Game Strike Authorization (Variety)

title: How Samsung’s Galaxy S24 Ultra Will Change Smartphones Forever
text:
Updated January 10: article originally posted January 7.
The upcoming Galaxy Unpacked event will set the standard for every flagship phone in 2024 to be measured against. The Galaxy S24 Ultra is Samsung’s bid to define the future of smartphones.
First, the Galaxy S24 Ultra must be the proverbial “really good phone.” There should be no obvious mistakes, nothing weaker than the opposition, and essentially everything a consumer expected from the leading Android flagship must be in the Galaxy S24 Ultra. Samsung’s iterative approach to the Ultra handsets means that the success of the S23 Ultra should easily carry on with the requisite upgrades in the specifications.
It’s also worth remembering that the S24 Ultra is part of a family of phones. There is a halo effect with the Galaxy S24 branding, which means the Galaxy S24 and Galaxy S24+ handsets also need to be up to standard—any issues with the handset lower down the portfolio will impact the S24 Ultra.
That’s one reason why the community is sensitive to the disparity between the Exynos and the Snapdragon chipsets used by the lower-tier models. Luckily for those wanting the ultimate power, the S24 Ultra will exclusively run the more respected Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 for Samsung.
Samsung’s popularity, interest from the press, and leadership role in the Android space will ensure the Galaxy S24 Ultra will be seen as the handset to beat for future flagships.
Update: Monday January 8. During the company's CES Press Conference, Samsung outlined its wider vision of AI in technology. Titled “AI For All - Connectivity In The Age Of AI,” Samsung Device Experience CEO Jong-He ‘JH’ Han introduced several partners and devices that will bring AI to consumers.
The traditional meme of the Internet Connected Fridge has been updated with the "Refrigerator With AI Family Hub,” offering a 32-inch display reporting on the products the AI recognizes inside the fridge with recipe suggestions and tracking of use-by dates. A similar AI hub is part of the Laundry Combo, offering AI in a washer and dryer.
On the consumer electronics side, Samsung took the opportunity to showcase the AI features in its recently launched Galaxy Book4 laptop. While there was no specific mention of the Galaxy S24 family, the entire presentation had a smartphone-shaped hole in it.
A hole that will be packed by the upcoming Galaxy Unpacked event.
Update: Wednesday January 10. Mihai Matei reports on the latest push by the South Korean company to prepare the market for the upcoming explosion of AI around the Samsung Galaxy brand, and it’s all focused on one location.
The architecturally ambitious Las Vegas Sphere, with its massive LED surface, was briefly taken over by a partnership between Samsung and Marvel’s “What If” series, with the upcoming addition to the Galaxy S range, promoted across the sky. As Samsung puts it; “A new era is coming with Galaxy AI.”
With the “AI for All” presentation addressed to the industry and the media at CES earlier this week, the Las Vegas promotion reaches out to consumers. The question now is how much AI Samsung will deliver, and how effective it will be.
The upcoming Galaxy Unpacked event will lean heavily toward using artificial intelligence on the smartphone. If you haven't seen the signs, the invitation screaming "Galaxy AI is coming” gives the game away. The South Korean company is not going into the event cold. Its Samsung Gauss AI system was given an official launch at the end of 2023
Several specific AI features have already been trailed around the camera, Zoom with Galaxy AI was showcased in the teaser videos ahead of the Galaxy Unpacked events. More importantly, both Qualcomm and Samsung have ensured that the respective Snapdragon and Exynos chipsets have dedicated hardware to enhance AI and ML software routines.
Samsung’s Exynos joins and reinforces Qualcomm’s snapdragon, MediaTek's Dimensity, and Google’s Tensor in offering hardware support for AI and ML routines. That means the Galaxy S24, S24+, and S24 Ultra handsets—which could easily have used a different vision of hardware to achieve AI—will consolidate the market. This is how AI can be delivered across the Android ecosystem.
In all this, do not discount how comfortable consumers are buying a Samsung device. While Google’s launch of the Pixel 8 and Pixel 8 Pro handsets was built around the promise of AI, the market share of Pixel devices and Galaxy devices are not in the same ballpark. Samsung can bring AI to the broadest possible market around the world.
Consumers who walk into a store to “buy a new Samsung” will have AI in their hands, first with the S24 family and then throughout the year into the new Galaxy A handsets and the Galaxy Tabs. The practical impact of AI on photography will be part of OneUI, and the “Galaxy AI” will no doubt be mentioned throughout the launch and at every point-of-sale unit.
There’s another area where Samsung can set the standard going forward. The company could match Google’s promise of seven years of software and security updates across the Galaxy S range. Google has shown how attractive this is; now, Samsung can force itself to the front of the line in the broader consumer market.
Samsung’s focus on delivering AI, consumer confidence in the brand, and an extended support window for software and hardware is how the Galaxy S24 can shape the smartphone world in 2024.
